cardiovascular.name: Cardiovascular System
cardiovascular.summary: The heart and blood vessels that circulate blood, delivering oxygen and nutrients while removing metabolic waste.

physiology.heading: The Cardiac Cycle: Pressure-Volume Mechanics
points: The cardiac cycle divides into diastole (ventricular relaxation and filling) and systole (contraction and ejection); atrial contraction always precedes ventricular contraction, and although right- and left-heart pressures differ substantially, both sides move through an identical sequence of phases in parallel.

Isovolumetric contraction begins the instant ventricular pressure exceeds atrial pressure, snapping the AV valves shut (generating S1); because both AV and semilunar valves are transiently closed, ventricular volume cannot change even as pressure rises steeply — hence 'isovolumetric.' Contraction continues until ventricular pressure exceeds aortic (or pulmonary) pressure, at which point the semilunar valves open and the ejection phase begins.

Ejection itself has a rapid phase (roughly the first third, driven by the large pressure gradient between ventricle and great vessel) followed by a slower reduced-ejection phase as the pressure gradient narrows; only about 60% of end-diastolic volume is normally ejected per beat (the ejection fraction), leaving a residual end-systolic volume.

Isovolumetric relaxation follows semilunar valve closure (S2, occurring when ventricular pressure falls below aortic/pulmonary pressure) and lasts until ventricular pressure drops below atrial pressure, again with all four valves shut and no volume change.

Filling then proceeds through a rapid phase (large AV pressure gradient immediately after AV valve opening), a slower diastasis phase (as atrial and ventricular pressures equilibrate), and a final atrial contraction ('atrial kick') that contributes roughly the last 20% of end-diastolic volume — a contribution that becomes hemodynamically important when ventricular compliance is reduced, and is lost entirely in atrial fibrillation.

These phases are conventionally represented on a Wiggers diagram, superimposing aortic pressure, ventricular pressure, atrial pressure, ventricular volume, the ECG trace, and phonocardiogram (heart sounds) on a shared time axis — and on the pressure-volume (P-V) loop, where the enclosed area directly represents stroke work and the loop's width along the volume axis represents stroke volume.

physiology.heading: Determinants of Stroke Volume and Cardiac Output
points: Cardiac output (CO) = heart rate × stroke volume. Stroke volume is set by three interacting variables: preload, afterload, and contractility, each of which can be visualized as shifting the ventricular pressure-volume loop.

Preload corresponds operationally to end-diastolic volume (or, more precisely, end-diastolic sarcomere length/wall stress). The Frank-Starling mechanism describes how increasing preload increases stroke volume: stretching the sarcomere toward its optimal length increases the number of actin-myosin cross-bridge interactions possible and increases the Ca2+ sensitivity of troponin C (length-dependent activation, partly mediated by the giant sarcomeric protein titin) — meaning greater venous return produces a proportionally stronger contraction without requiring any change in intrinsic contractility.

Afterload is the wall stress the ventricle must generate to open the semilunar valve and eject blood, closely approximated clinically by aortic pressure or systemic vascular resistance for the left ventricle. Afterload is inversely related to stroke volume: at a fixed preload and contractility, raising afterload leaves more blood in the ventricle at end-systole (increasing end-systolic volume) and reduces the volume ejected.

Contractility (inotropy) is the force-generating capacity of the myocardium independent of loading conditions, governed principally by the availability of intracellular calcium during excitation-contraction coupling. Sympathetic stimulation increases contractility via beta-1 adrenergic receptor activation of protein kinase A, which phosphorylates L-type calcium channels (increasing Ca2+ influx), phospholamban (accelerating SERCA-mediated Ca2+ reuptake and thus relaxation — the lusitropic effect), and troponin I (reducing Ca2+ affinity, also aiding relaxation).

Heart rate reflects the intrinsic firing rate of the sinoatrial node, continuously modulated by autonomic tone: sympathetic input (norepinephrine acting on beta-1 receptors) accelerates the rate of diastolic (phase 4) depolarization in pacemaker cells, while vagal input (acetylcholine acting on M2 muscarinic receptors) hyperpolarizes pacemaker cells and slows phase 4 depolarization, lowering heart rate; resting heart rate is normally dominated by vagal tone.

physiology.heading: Cardiac Action Potentials and Excitation-Contraction Coupling
points: The ventricular myocyte action potential has five phases. Phase 4 is the stable resting membrane potential (~-90 mV), dominated by high resting K+ permeability through inward-rectifier channels (IK1). Phase 0 is rapid depolarization: once threshold is reached, fast voltage-gated Na+ channels open, producing a steep influx of Na+ (INa) that drives the membrane rapidly toward +50 mV — this steep upstroke is what allows rapid, coordinated propagation through the myocardium.

Phase 1 is early, partial repolarization caused by fast inactivation of Na+ channels combined with a transient outward K+ current (Ito). Phase 2, the plateau, is the defining feature of cardiac (versus neuronal or skeletal muscle) action potentials: sustained Ca2+ influx through L-type ('long-lasting') voltage-gated calcium channels roughly balances ongoing K+ efflux, holding the membrane near 0 mV for 100-200 ms. This prolonged plateau (and the resulting long refractory period) prevents the heart from being tetanized — ensuring each contraction is followed by mechanical relaxation and diastolic filling before the next beat can occur.

Phase 3 is repolarization: as L-type Ca2+ channels inactivate, outward K+ currents (chiefly the delayed rectifiers IKr and IKs) dominate and return the membrane to resting potential, closing the cycle. Genetic or pharmacological disruption of these repolarizing K+ currents underlies acquired and congenital long QT syndromes and associated arrhythmia risk.

Excitation-contraction coupling (ECC) links the electrical action potential to mechanical contraction via calcium-induced calcium release (CICR). The Ca2+ that enters through L-type channels during phase 2 does not itself directly trigger contraction in significant quantity — instead, it acts as a trigger that binds ryanodine receptors (RyR2) on the adjacent sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR), causing the SR to release a much larger quantity of stored Ca2+ into the cytosol (roughly 75% of the Ca2+ that drives contraction comes from the SR, not the extracellular space).

Cytosolic Ca2+ then binds troponin C, causing a conformational shift that displaces tropomyosin away from the myosin-binding sites on actin. This exposes the binding sites, allowing myosin cross-bridges to form and cycle (powered by ATP hydrolysis) — the sliding-filament mechanism of contraction, structurally identical to skeletal muscle at the sarcomere level.

Relaxation (lusitropy) requires cytosolic Ca2+ to fall, achieved primarily by the SERCA2a pump (sarco/endoplasmic reticulum Ca2+-ATPase) actively resequestering Ca2+ into the SR, with a smaller contribution from the sarcolemmal Na+/Ca2+ exchanger extruding Ca2+ from the cell. SERCA2a activity is itself regulated by phospholamban, which inhibits the pump at baseline; PKA-mediated phosphorylation of phospholamban (via beta-adrenergic stimulation) relieves this inhibition, accelerating both Ca2+ reuptake and myocardial relaxation.

physiology.heading: The Cardiac Conduction System
points: The sinoatrial (SA) node — a crescent-shaped cluster of specialized myocytes at the junction of the crista terminalis and superior vena cava — is the heart's dominant pacemaker because its cells lack a stable resting potential. Instead, T-type calcium channels produce a slow spontaneous depolarization ('funny current'/pacemaker potential) during phase 4, which continues until it reaches the threshold for L-type calcium channels, firing an action potential; notably, pacemaker cell depolarization (unlike working myocardium) is carried predominantly by calcium rather than sodium current.

From the SA node, the impulse spreads across atrial myocardium and converges on the atrioventricular (AV) node, situated within the interatrial septum at the Koch triangle. AV nodal conduction is deliberately slow — corresponding to the ECG's PR interval — which delays ventricular activation long enough for atrial contraction to complete ventricular filling before the ventricles depolarize.

Beyond the AV node, the impulse enters the bundle of His, then the left and right bundle branches, and finally the extensive Purkinje fiber network. Purkinje fibers conduct considerably faster than ordinary myocardium, ensuring the ventricles depolarize in a coordinated, near-simultaneous wave (activation spreading from apex to base and endocardium to epicardium) rather than a slow, disorganized spread that would produce weak, uncoordinated contraction.

Because the SA node has the fastest intrinsic firing rate, it normally suppresses the automaticity of subsidiary pacemakers (the AV node and Purkinje fibers) through overdrive suppression. If the SA node fails, the AV node (intrinsic rate ~40-60/min) or ventricular Purkinje tissue (intrinsic rate ~20-40/min) can assume pacemaker function at progressively slower rates — the physiological basis of escape rhythms.

physiology.heading: Hemodynamics and Vascular Resistance
points: Blood flow (Q) through the vasculature follows the same principles governing any fluid in a tube: Q = ΔP/R (analogous to Ohm's law), where ΔP is the pressure gradient driving flow and R is vascular resistance opposing it.

By Poiseuille's law, resistance is inversely proportional to the fourth power of vessel radius (R ∝ 1/r⁴) — meaning even small changes in arteriolar diameter produce large changes in resistance. This makes arterioles, which possess substantial smooth muscle and can markedly change caliber, the principal site of resistance regulation in the entire circulation.

Mean pressure falls progressively along the circuit — aorta to large arteries to arterioles to capillaries to venules to veins — but the steepest single drop occurs across the arterioles, consistent with their dominant contribution to total peripheral resistance. Arteriolar vasoconstriction raises upstream (arterial) pressure while reducing downstream capillary flow; vasodilation has the opposite effect, the fundamental basis of both local (autoregulatory, metabolic) and systemic (autonomic) blood flow control.

Capillary exchange of fluid is governed by Starling forces: hydrostatic pressure (favoring filtration out of the capillary) opposed by plasma oncotic pressure (favoring reabsorption, driven mainly by plasma proteins, especially albumin). Net filtration versus reabsorption at any point along the capillary depends on the balance of these opposing pressures, and any imbalance can produce net fluid accumulation in the interstitium — edema (see Capillary Fluid Exchange below for the full quantitative treatment).

physiology.heading: Blood Pressure Regulation
points: Systolic pressure is the peak arterial pressure during ventricular ejection; diastolic pressure is the trough pressure during ventricular relaxation/filling. Mean arterial pressure (MAP) — the average pressure driving tissue perfusion — is approximately diastolic pressure plus one-third of pulse pressure, and is fundamentally the product of cardiac output and systemic vascular resistance (MAP ≈ CO × SVR).

Short-term (second-to-second) regulation is dominated by the baroreceptor reflex. Stretch-sensitive baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch fire tonically, increasing their firing rate as arterial wall distension increases with rising pressure. Afferent signals travel via the glossopharyngeal nerve (from the carotid sinus) and vagus nerve (from the aortic arch) to the nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) in the medulla.

Increased baroreceptor firing (rising pressure) drives the NTS to excite the nucleus ambiguus, increasing vagal (parasympathetic) inhibitory output to the SA node — slowing heart rate — while simultaneously inhibiting sympathetic outflow from the rostral ventrolateral medulla, reducing peripheral vasoconstriction and cardiac contractility. A fall in pressure produces the mirror-image response: reduced baroreceptor firing disinhibits sympathetic outflow and reduces vagal tone, raising heart rate, contractility, and vascular resistance to restore pressure.

Longer-term regulation (minutes to days) is dominated by the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS). Reduced renal perfusion pressure, reduced NaCl delivery to the macula densa, or beta-1 adrenergic stimulation trigger juxtaglomerular cells to release renin, which cleaves angiotensinogen (hepatic in origin) to angiotensin I; angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE, chiefly in pulmonary vascular endothelium) then converts this to angiotensin II.

Angiotensin II is a potent direct vasoconstrictor and also stimulates the adrenal cortex (zona glomerulosa) to secrete aldosterone, which increases distal nephron sodium (and secondary water) reabsorption — expanding plasma volume and raising blood pressure over a longer timescale than the baroreceptor reflex allows. Circulating angiotensin II additionally modulates baroreflex sensitivity via AT1 receptors in the area postrema and NTS, resetting the reflex toward higher pressures during RAAS activation.

physiology.heading: Cardiac Energetics and Coronary Circulation
points: Myocardial oxygen demand is set by three principal variables: heart rate, contractility, and ventricular wall stress (tension). Of these, heart rate is generally considered the most influential, since a faster rate both increases the number of contractions per minute and — critically — shortens diastole, the phase during which the left ventricle actually receives most of its blood supply.

Wall stress is formalized by the Law of Laplace: wall stress is proportional to ventricular pressure × radius, divided by wall thickness (σ ∝ P·r/h). This explains why a dilated, thin-walled ventricle generates more wall tension (and thus consumes more oxygen) for a given pressure than a normally sized or compensatorily hypertrophied one.

Uniquely among vascular beds, left ventricular coronary blood flow is predominantly diastolic rather than systolic: during systole, contracting myocardium mechanically compresses the intramural coronary microvessels (most severely in the subendocardium), impeding inflow, whereas diastolic relaxation releases this compression and allows the bulk of coronary filling to occur. Approximately 70-80% of left ventricular flow occurs in diastole, compared to a roughly even systolic/diastolic split in the lower-pressure right ventricle.

Coronary perfusion pressure (CPP) is approximated as aortic diastolic pressure minus left ventricular end-diastolic pressure (CPP = DBP − LVEDP). Tachycardia disproportionately shortens diastole (relative to systole), directly reducing the time available for coronary filling — a key reason rapid heart rates can precipitate subendocardial ischemia even without any change in coronary artery diameter.

At rest the myocardium already extracts 60-80% of the oxygen delivered by coronary blood — a far higher extraction fraction than most other tissues — meaning the heart has very limited capacity to meet increased demand by extracting more oxygen from a fixed blood supply. Instead, increased demand must be met almost entirely by increasing coronary blood flow itself, chiefly through metabolic vasodilation (adenosine release from ATP-consuming myocytes is a principal mediator) acting on coronary arteriolar smooth muscle, a mechanism termed coronary flow reserve.

physiology.heading: Venous Return and Integration with Cardiac Function
points: Guyton's model frames venous return as a function of the pressure gradient between mean systemic filling pressure (MSFP — the pressure that would exist throughout the systemic circulation if the heart stopped and pressure equilibrated) and right atrial pressure (RAP), divided by the resistance to venous return: VR = (MSFP − RAP) / RVR.

MSFP is determined by total circulating blood volume and venous compliance/tone; because roughly 60-70% of total blood volume resides in the highly compliant venous system at any time, changes in venous tone (via sympathetic venoconstriction) can substantially and rapidly alter effective circulating (stressed) volume without any change in actual blood volume — 'auto-transfusing' blood from unstressed venous reservoirs into the active circulation.

Plotting venous return against right atrial pressure produces the vascular function curve, which can be superimposed on the cardiac function (Frank-Starling) curve — plotting cardiac output against right atrial pressure — on the same axes. Because venous return must equal cardiac output at steady state, the intersection of these two curves defines the system's actual operating point for right atrial pressure and cardiac output.

This integrated framework explains phenomena that considering the heart in isolation cannot: for example, why hemorrhage (which lowers MSFP by reducing stressed volume) reduces cardiac output even in an otherwise-healthy heart, and why positive-pressure mechanical ventilation (which raises intrathoracic and right atrial pressure) can reduce venous return and cardiac output independent of any change in cardiac contractility.

physiology.heading: Local (Intrinsic) Regulation of Blood Flow
points: Beyond centralized autonomic/hormonal control, individual vascular beds regulate their own blood flow locally to match tissue metabolic demand — a property especially critical in the coronary, cerebral, and renal circulations.

Metabolic (or 'active hyperemia') regulation: increased tissue metabolic activity elevates local concentrations of vasodilator metabolites — adenosine, CO2, H+, K+, and reduced local pO2 — which relax arteriolar smooth muscle and increase flow to match the tissue's current metabolic rate. This is the principal mechanism behind coronary flow reserve and exercise-induced skeletal muscle hyperemia.

Myogenic regulation: vascular smooth muscle intrinsically contracts in response to stretch and relaxes when stretch is reduced, independent of any neural or hormonal input. This provides moment-to-moment protection against pressure-driven over-perfusion and is a major contributor to autoregulation — the capacity of an organ to maintain relatively constant blood flow across a range of perfusion pressures.

Endothelium-derived regulation: vascular endothelium is not a passive lining but an active paracrine signaling layer. Endothelial cells synthesize nitric oxide (NO, via endothelial NO synthase, stimulated by shear stress and various agonists) and prostacyclin, both potent vasodilators; they also produce endothelin-1, one of the most potent endogenous vasoconstrictors known. The balance of these endothelium-derived factors is a key determinant of vascular tone and is disrupted ('endothelial dysfunction') in atherosclerosis, diabetes, and hypertension.

physiology.heading: Capillary Fluid Exchange and Lymphatic Return
points: Fluid movement across the capillary wall is governed by the Starling equation: Jv = Kf[(Pc − Pi) − σ(πc − πi)], where Jv is net filtration, Kf is the filtration coefficient (capillary permeability × surface area), Pc and Pi are capillary and interstitial hydrostatic pressures, πc and πi are capillary and interstitial oncotic pressures, and σ is the reflection coefficient (how effectively the capillary wall restricts protein passage).

Capillary hydrostatic pressure typically favors filtration (fluid moving out of the capillary into the interstitium) at the arteriolar end, while plasma oncotic pressure (chiefly from albumin) opposes it; classical teaching held that pressure reverses toward net reabsorption at the venular end, though modern evidence suggests most capillary beds filter net fluid along their entire length under normal conditions, with the interstitium relying on lymphatic drainage — not venular reabsorption — to return the bulk of filtered fluid to the circulation.

The lymphatic system thus functions as an essential overflow return pathway: filtered interstitial fluid (now called lymph) is collected by blind-ended lymphatic capillaries, propelled centrally through progressively larger lymphatic vessels (aided by one-way valves and surrounding skeletal muscle contraction, since lymphatics have no central pump), and ultimately returned to the venous circulation via the thoracic duct and right lymphatic duct. Impaired lymphatic drainage, or filtration that outpaces lymphatic capacity, produces edema.

histology.heading: Cardiac Muscle Ultrastructure
points: Cardiac muscle (myocardium) is striated, like skeletal muscle, containing organized sarcomeres with the same actin-myosin banding pattern (A-bands, I-bands, Z-lines) visible under light microscopy — but cardiomyocytes differ from skeletal fibers in being shorter, branching, and typically mononucleated (occasionally binucleated) rather than long, unbranched, and multinucleated.

Neighboring cardiomyocytes are joined end-to-end at intercalated discs, which appear as dark transverse (sometimes stepped/zig-zag) lines on light microscopy. Ultrastructurally, intercalated discs contain three distinct junction types arranged regionally: fascia adherens and desmosomes concentrate at the transverse ('plicate') segments running perpendicular to the fiber and anchor actin filaments/intermediate filaments at the Z-line level, providing mechanical coupling; gap junctions concentrate at the longitudinal ('interplicate') segments and provide direct low-resistance electrical coupling between cells.

The gap junctions of the intercalated disc give cardiac muscle the functional property of a syncytium: despite being histologically composed of discrete, individually membrane-bound cells, electrical excitation passes directly cell-to-cell through connexin channels, allowing an entire chamber to depolarize and contract as a single coordinated unit.

Cardiomyocytes contain unusually abundant, large mitochondria packed between myofibrils — reflecting the myocardium's continuous, high-volume ATP demand and near-total reliance on oxidative phosphorylation — along with an extensive T-tubule system (wider and more centrally organized than in skeletal muscle, aligned at the Z-line) that allows the action potential to trigger near-synchronous Ca2+ release throughout the cell's depth.

Troponin C, I, and T mediate the calcium-dependent regulation of cross-bridge cycling described in excitation-contraction coupling; cardiac-specific isoforms of troponin I and T are released into circulation following myocardial injury and serve as the principal clinical biomarkers for diagnosing myocardial infarction.

histology.heading: Conduction System Histology
points: Pacemaker cells of the SA and AV nodes are histologically distinct from working (contractile) myocardium: smaller in diameter, with sparse and disorganized myofibrils and correspondingly faint striation, reflecting a cellular specialization for automaticity and impulse generation rather than forceful contraction.

Purkinje fibers, located in the subendocardium, are notably larger than ordinary cardiomyocytes with pale-staining cytoplasm; their myofibrils are sparse and confined to the cell periphery, while the central cytoplasm is dominated by abundant glycogen stores — an architecture that favors rapid conduction velocity over contractile force generation, allowing the ventricles to be activated almost simultaneously.

histology.heading: Blood Vessel Wall Histology
points: Most blood vessels share a common three-layer wall architecture — an inner tunica intima, a middle tunica media, and an outer tunica adventitia (externa) — though the relative thickness, cellular composition, and elastic content of each layer vary considerably between arteries, veins, and capillaries.

The tunica intima consists of a single layer of simple squamous endothelial cells resting on a basal lamina. Endothelium may be continuous (tight intercellular junctions, found in most tissues including the blood-brain barrier), fenestrated (containing transcellular pores, found in renal glomeruli, choroid plexus, and intestinal mucosa to permit rapid filtration or absorption), or discontinuous (with true intercellular gaps, found in hepatic, splenic, and bone marrow sinusoids to allow passage of cells and large macromolecules).

The tunica media consists of circumferentially or diagonally arranged smooth muscle cells embedded in an extracellular matrix of collagen and elastin, separated from the intima by the internal elastic lamina. This layer is markedly thicker in arteries than veins at any comparable caliber, and is thickest of all in large elastic (conducting) arteries such as the aorta, whose abundant elastic lamellae stretch during systolic ejection and recoil during diastole — the Windkessel effect — converting pulsatile ventricular output into steadier downstream flow.

Muscular (distributing) arteries, by contrast, have proportionally more smooth muscle and less elastin in the media, reflecting their role in actively regulating regional blood flow via vasoconstriction/vasodilation rather than passive elastic recoil. Veins, especially in the limbs, additionally contain intraluminal valves — folds of the tunica intima that prevent retrograde flow and work with the surrounding skeletal muscle pump to assist venous return against gravity.

The tunica adventitia is composed predominantly of collagen (with variable elastin), anchoring the vessel to surrounding connective tissue and — in vessels thick enough that luminal diffusion cannot adequately nourish the outer wall — housing the vasa vasorum and nervi vasorum, the small nutrient vessels and autonomic nerve fibers that supply the vessel wall itself.

Capillaries, the primary site of gas, nutrient, and fluid exchange, consist of only endothelium and basal lamina (a tunica intima alone, without media or adventitia) — a minimal structure that reduces diffusion distance to the surrounding tissue, at the cost of any independent contractile or structural reinforcement.

histology.heading: Cardiac Wall Layers and Pericardium
points: The heart wall comprises three layers: the epicardium (outermost, the visceral layer of serous pericardium — a single mesothelial layer over connective tissue and adipose tissue that houses the coronary vessels and cardiac nerves), the myocardium (the thick, muscular middle layer described above), and the endocardium (innermost, a single layer of simple squamous endothelium over a thin connective tissue layer, continuous with the endothelial lining of all connected blood vessels).

The pericardium as a whole consists of a fibrous outer layer (dense connective tissue, anchoring the heart within the mediastinum and limiting acute over-distension) and a serous inner layer with two divisions: the parietal pericardium (lining the fibrous sac) and visceral pericardium/epicardium (adherent to the heart surface). The potential space between parietal and visceral layers — the pericardial cavity — normally contains a thin film of serous fluid that minimizes friction during the cardiac cycle, drained by a rich local lymphatic network.

The fibrous cardiac skeleton — dense connective tissue forming the annuli fibrosi (rings encircling each valve), trigona fibrosi, and the membranous interventricular septum — electrically insulates the atria from the ventricles (forcing all normal conduction through the AV node), provides rigid anchor points for valve leaflets, and serves as the origin/insertion for atrial and ventricular myocardial fibers.

histology.heading: Cardiac Valve Histology
points: Cardiac valve leaflets are avascular beyond their proximal attachment and are covered by a continuous layer of valve endothelial cells, histologically and functionally continuous with the endocardium. Beneath this endothelium, the leaflet stroma is organized into distinct layers populated by valve interstitial cells — quiescent fibroblast-like cells responsible for extracellular matrix maintenance, which can pathologically differentiate into osteoblast-like cells and drive dystrophic valve calcification in degenerative valve disease.

Atrioventricular (mitral, tricuspid) valves are classically described with three to four layers: the atrialis (facing the atrium, aligned collagen and elastic fibers), the spongiosa (loosely organized proteoglycan- and glycosaminoglycan-rich tissue that allows shear and cushions leaflet flexure), the fibrosa (the mechanically dominant layer, dense circumferentially-oriented collagen continuous with the fibrous skeleton, providing the leaflet's tensile strength), and a ventricularis (facing the ventricle, elastin-rich, supporting elastic recoil). In the AV valves, the fibrosa continues into the chordae tendineae — dense regular connective tissue cords anchoring the leaflet free edges to the papillary muscles.

Semilunar (aortic, pulmonic) valves show an analogous layered organization, typically described as arterialis, fibrosa, spongiosa, and ventricularis; the fibrosa again provides the principal load-bearing structure, while the elastin-rich ventricularis/arterialis layers support the rapid, repeated recoil these valves undergo with every cardiac cycle.

histology.heading: Excitation-Contraction Coupling Ultrastructure
points: The physical basis of calcium-induced calcium release is a specialized junctional structure called the dyad (or couplon): a close physical apposition between the T-tubule membrane (bearing L-type calcium channels/dihydropyridine receptors) and the terminal cisternae of the adjacent sarcoplasmic reticulum (bearing clusters of ryanodine receptors), separated by only a narrow diadic cleft of roughly 12-15 nanometers.

This tight spatial coupling allows the relatively small Ca2+ influx through L-type channels during the action potential plateau to reach a very high local concentration within the diadic cleft, sufficient to reliably trigger ryanodine receptor opening and the much larger, amplifying SR calcium release — despite the trigger current itself being far too small to raise bulk cytosolic calcium to contraction-triggering levels on its own.

Because cardiac T-tubules are wider and more centrally distributed than their skeletal muscle counterparts (with dyads, rather than skeletal muscle's triads, at each junction), and because SR calcium stores in cardiac muscle are comparatively less extensive than in skeletal muscle, cardiac contraction remains fundamentally more dependent on trigger calcium entering from the extracellular space — a key reason cardiac muscle, unlike skeletal muscle, cannot contract in the complete absence of extracellular calcium.

nervous.name: Nervous System
nervous.summary: The brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves that generate, transmit, and integrate electrical and chemical signals throughout the body.

physiology.heading: Resting Membrane Potential and Ionic Basis of Excitability
points: Neurons maintain a resting membrane potential of approximately -60 to -70 mV (inside relative to outside), generated by the combined effect of unequal ion concentration gradients (Na+ and Ca2+ concentrated extracellularly; K+ concentrated intracellularly, maintained against their gradients by the Na+/K+-ATPase) and the membrane's selective permeability to these ions.

At rest, the membrane is far more permeable to K+ than Na+ due to a much higher density of open K+ leak channels; because permeability dominates the resting potential's value (as described by the Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz equation, which weights each ion's equilibrium potential by its relative membrane permeability), the resting membrane sits close to the K+ equilibrium potential rather than midway between the Na+ and K+ equilibrium potentials.

The Na+/K+-ATPase is electrogenic (pumping 3 Na+ out for every 2 K+ in per cycle), directly contributing a small hyperpolarizing component to the resting potential in addition to its essential role in maintaining the concentration gradients that the leak channels depend on.

physiology.heading: Action Potential Generation and Propagation
points: An action potential is triggered when depolarizing input (typically summed postsynaptic potentials arriving at the axon hillock, the region of highest voltage-gated Na+ channel density) brings the membrane to threshold (~-55 mV), opening voltage-gated Na+ channels.

Depolarization (rising phase) results from a large, rapid Na+ influx down its electrochemical gradient, driving the membrane potential from rest toward +30 mV; this phase is regenerative and all-or-nothing — once threshold is crossed, the action potential proceeds to its full amplitude regardless of further stimulus strength.

Repolarization follows as voltage-gated Na+ channels inactivate (a time-dependent process distinct from their voltage-dependent activation gate) and voltage-gated K+ channels — slower to open than Na+ channels — activate, driving K+ efflux that returns the membrane toward rest; K+ channels typically remain open slightly longer than needed, producing a brief afterhyperpolarization before the resting potential is re-established.

The refractory period has two components: the absolute refractory period (Na+ channels inactivated and incapable of reopening regardless of stimulus strength, corresponding roughly to the depolarization and repolarization phases) and the relative refractory period (Na+ channels have recovered from inactivation but the membrane remains hyperpolarized, so a stronger-than-normal stimulus is needed to reach threshold). Refractory periods enforce unidirectional propagation (preventing the action potential from re-triggering the region it just depolarized) and cap the maximum firing frequency of a neuron.

In myelinated axons, action potentials propagate via saltatory conduction: because myelin insulates the internodal membrane and prevents ionic current leakage, voltage-gated Na+ channels — clustered at the exposed nodes of Ranvier — are the only points where the action potential must actively regenerate, allowing the depolarization to effectively 'jump' node to node. This dramatically increases conduction velocity and reduces metabolic cost (less membrane area requires active ion pumping) relative to continuous conduction in unmyelinated axons of the same diameter.

physiology.heading: Synaptic Transmission
points: At a chemical synapse, an arriving presynaptic action potential depolarizes the axon terminal, opening voltage-gated Ca2+ channels; Ca2+ influx triggers synaptic vesicles (pre-docked at the active zone via SNARE proteins) to fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release neurotransmitter into the synaptic cleft by exocytosis.

Released neurotransmitter diffuses across the cleft and binds postsynaptic receptors, which are broadly either ionotropic (ligand-gated ion channels producing fast, brief postsynaptic potentials by directly altering membrane permeability) or metabotropic (G-protein-coupled receptors producing slower, longer-lasting effects via second-messenger cascades).

Postsynaptic potentials are graded (not all-or-nothing, unlike axonal action potentials) and summate — spatially (from multiple simultaneously active synapses) and temporally (from repeated activation of the same synapse in rapid succession) — at the postsynaptic neuron's axon hillock, determining whether threshold is reached and a new action potential fires.

Neurotransmitter action is terminated by reuptake (via presynaptic transporters, recycling neurotransmitter for repackaging — the target of drugs such as SSRIs), enzymatic degradation (e.g., acetylcholinesterase rapidly hydrolyzing acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft), or simple diffusion away from the synapse — the specific termination mechanism varying by neurotransmitter.

physiology.heading: Major Neurotransmitter Systems and Receptor Pharmacology
points: Glutamate is the principal excitatory neurotransmitter in the central nervous system, acting on both ionotropic receptors (AMPA, NMDA, and kainate — all ligand-gated cation channels) and metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluRs, G-protein-coupled, modulating cell signaling more slowly). AMPA receptors mediate fast excitatory transmission at most glutamatergic synapses, opening rapidly upon glutamate binding to allow Na+ influx.

The NMDA receptor is functionally distinctive: it requires both glutamate binding and postsynaptic depolarization to open, because at resting potential its channel pore is physically blocked by extracellular Mg2+ — a block only relieved once the membrane is sufficiently depolarized (typically by concurrent AMPA receptor activity). This makes the NMDA receptor a coincidence detector, opening only when presynaptic glutamate release and postsynaptic depolarization occur together, and its resulting Ca2+ influx (NMDA receptors are highly Ca2+-permeable) is central to long-term potentiation, synaptic plasticity, and memory formation.

GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid) is the principal inhibitory neurotransmitter in the CNS, synthesized from glutamate by glutamic acid decarboxylase. GABA-A receptors are ionotropic chloride channels — GABA binding opens the channel, Cl- influx hyperpolarizes the cell, producing an inhibitory postsynaptic potential; GABA-A receptors are the molecular target of benzodiazepines and barbiturates, which act as positive allosteric modulators to increase channel opening frequency/duration respectively. GABA-B receptors are metabotropic, acting via G-proteins on a slower timescale.

Beyond glutamate and GABA, several neuromodulatory systems project diffusely from discrete brainstem/midbrain nuclei to broad forebrain territories: dopaminergic neurons (substantia nigra, ventral tegmental area) modulate motor control, reward, and executive function; serotonergic neurons (raphe nuclei) modulate mood, sleep, and appetite; noradrenergic neurons (locus coeruleus) modulate arousal and attention. These systems typically act through metabotropic (G-protein-coupled) receptors, producing widespread modulatory rather than point-to-point signaling effects.

physiology.heading: Cerebral Cortex: Functional Organization
points: The cerebral cortex is divided into four lobes per hemisphere. The frontal lobe governs motor function, language production, and executive processes (attention, working memory, planning, personality, social/moral reasoning); the primary motor cortex (precentral gyrus, Brodmann area 4) initiates voluntary movement, with the amount of cortex devoted to each body part corresponding to the fineness of motor control required — disproportionately large territory for the hands, face, and lips — classically depicted as the motor homunculus, though modern mapping suggests overlapping, action-type representations rather than a strict one-to-one map.

The parietal lobe processes somatosensory information; the primary somatosensory cortex (postcentral gyrus, Brodmann areas 3, 1, 2) receives thalamic input and interprets touch, pressure, vibration, pain, and temperature, with a similarly disproportionate sensory homunculus. The posterior parietal lobe (superior and inferior parietal lobules) integrates this sensory information with visual and other modalities to support spatial awareness and motor planning.

The temporal lobe processes auditory information (primary auditory cortex, Brodmann areas 41/42) and, in the dominant hemisphere (left, in roughly 95% of people), houses Wernicke's area (posterior superior temporal gyrus, Brodmann area 22) — responsible for language comprehension. Damage here produces fluent but nonsensical speech with impaired comprehension (receptive/Wernicke's aphasia).
The occipital lobe is dedicated to visual processing, with the primary visual cortex (Brodmann area 17/V1) as the first cortical relay for visual input from the thalamus (lateral geniculate nucleus).

Broca's area (inferior frontal gyrus, Brodmann areas 44/45, dominant hemisphere) governs the motor production and articulation of speech; a bundle of white matter (the arcuate fasciculus) directly connects Broca's and Wernicke's areas, since fluent speech production requires continuous integration of comprehended language with motor output. Damage to Broca's area produces labored, non-fluent speech with relatively preserved comprehension (expressive/Broca's aphasia).

physiology.heading: Autonomic Nervous System
points: The autonomic nervous system regulates involuntary visceral function through two anatomically and pharmacologically distinct divisions — sympathetic and parasympathetic — that typically exert opposing (or complementary) effects on the same target organs.

Both divisions use a two-neuron efferent pathway: a preganglionic neuron (cell body in the CNS, always releasing acetylcholine onto nicotinic receptors at the ganglion) synapses onto a postganglionic neuron, which then innervates the target tissue. Parasympathetic postganglionic neurons release acetylcholine onto muscarinic receptors at the target organ; sympathetic postganglionic neurons predominantly release norepinephrine onto adrenergic receptors (with the notable exception of sympathetic innervation of sweat glands, which is cholinergic).

Sympathetic ganglia lie close to the spinal cord (paravertebral chain or nearby prevertebral ganglia), giving short preganglionic and long postganglionic fibers, allowing for widespread, diffuse activation; parasympathetic ganglia lie near or within the target organ itself, giving long preganglionic and short postganglionic fibers, allowing for more localized, discrete effects.

The adrenal medulla is a specialized exception: it is functionally a modified sympathetic ganglion, directly innervated by preganglionic sympathetic fibers, and releases epinephrine (and some norepinephrine) directly into the bloodstream as a hormone rather than via a discrete postganglionic synapse — allowing coordinated, body-wide sympathetic activation during acute stress.

physiology.heading: Cerebrospinal Fluid and the Blood-Brain Barrier
points: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) fills the brain ventricles and subarachnoid space, providing mechanical protection (buoyancy that reduces the brain's effective weight), nutrient delivery, and waste clearance. Total adult CSF volume is roughly 150 mL, but daily production is 400-600 mL — meaning the entire CSF volume is replaced 4-5 times per day.

CSF is produced predominantly by the choroid plexus, a highly vascularized structure of cuboidal epithelial cells (continuous with the ependymal lining of the ventricles) enclosing clusters of fenestrated capillaries. Unlike the tight, impermeable capillaries of the blood-brain barrier, choroid plexus capillaries are leaky — the actual barrier function (the blood-CSF barrier) is provided instead by tight junctions between the choroid epithelial cells themselves, which actively secrete CSF from their basolateral (blood-facing) side into the ventricular space.

CSF circulates from the lateral ventricles through the interventricular foramina into the third ventricle, through the cerebral aqueduct into the fourth ventricle, and then out into the subarachnoid space via the foramina of Luschka and Magendie, ultimately being reabsorbed into the venous circulation (classically via arachnoid villi, though extrachoroidal absorption routes are increasingly recognized).

The blood-brain barrier (BBB), distinct from the blood-CSF barrier, is formed by brain capillary endothelial cells joined by tight junctions (unlike the fenestrated, leaky capillaries typical elsewhere in the body), reinforced by a surrounding basement membrane, pericytes, and the perivascular end-feet of astrocytes. This barrier tightly restricts paracellular diffusion, forcing most substances to cross via specific transporters (e.g., GLUT1 for glucose) — protecting the CNS from circulating toxins and pathogens while still permitting essential nutrient delivery.

histology.heading: Neuron Structure
points: The neuronal cell body (soma/perikaryon) contains the nucleus and the biosynthetic machinery of the cell, including prominent Nissl bodies (rough endoplasmic reticulum arranged in stacks, visible as basophilic granules on light microscopy) reflecting the high protein synthetic demand of maintaining a large, metabolically active cell with extensive processes.

Dendrites are typically short, tapering, and highly branched, receiving synaptic input and often studded with dendritic spines — small membranous protrusions that serve as the primary postsynaptic site for excitatory synapses and are a major substrate for synaptic plasticity.

The axon arises from the axon hillock (a specialized region lacking Nissl substance, with the highest density of voltage-gated Na+ channels in the neuron) and can extend from micrometers to over a meter in length; axoplasmic transport (anterograde via kinesin motors, retrograde via dynein motors, along microtubule tracks) moves organelles, vesicles, and macromolecules between the soma and distant axon terminals — a process exploited by certain neurotropic pathogens and toxins to travel retrogradely into the CNS.

histology.heading: Glial Cells
points: Astrocytes, the most numerous CNS glial cell, are star-shaped cells with extensive branching processes; their perivascular 'end-feet' processes are a key structural component of the blood-brain barrier, and they additionally regulate extracellular K+ and neurotransmitter concentration, provide metabolic support to neurons, and contribute to synapse formation and modulation.

Oligodendrocytes are the CNS myelinating glia; unlike Schwann cells, a single oligodendrocyte extends multiple processes that each myelinate a segment of a different nearby axon (typically 20-60 internodal segments across multiple axons per cell), and oligodendrocytes lack the surrounding basal lamina present around Schwann cells.

Schwann cells are the PNS myelinating (and non-myelinating, ensheathing) glia; each myelinating Schwann cell wraps and myelinates only a single internodal segment of one axon (a 1:1 relationship, in contrast to the oligodendrocyte's 1:many arrangement), and is surrounded by its own basal lamina — a structural feature exploited during peripheral nerve regeneration, as the retained basal lamina tube guides regrowing axons back toward their original targets.

Microglia are the resident CNS immune cells (derived from yolk-sac myeloid progenitors rather than neuroectoderm, unlike other glia), performing continuous immune surveillance, phagocytosing debris and dead cells, and mediating neuroinflammatory responses to injury or infection.

Ependymal cells line the ventricular system and central canal of the spinal cord with a single layer of cuboidal-to-columnar, often ciliated epithelium, whose coordinated ciliary beating helps circulate CSF; specialized, modified ependymal cells of the choroid plexus produce cerebrospinal fluid.

histology.heading: Myelin and the Nodes of Ranvier
points: Myelin is a lipid-rich, multilamellar membrane wrapping formed by concentric layers of glial plasma membrane, providing electrical insulation that dramatically increases conduction velocity; compact myelin is periodically interrupted by Schmidt-Lanterman incisures (cytoplasmic pockets containing gap junctions, permitting limited exchange between the myelinating cell body and the innermost membrane layers).

Nodes of Ranvier are the short (~1 micrometer) unmyelinated gaps between adjacent myelin segments, where the axolemma is exposed to extracellular fluid and where voltage-gated Na+ channels are densely clustered — the structural basis for saltatory conduction.

Demyelinating disease illustrates the functional importance of this architecture: loss of myelin (as in multiple sclerosis, a CNS demyelinating disease, or Guillain-Barré syndrome, a PNS demyelinating disease) slows or blocks conduction by forcing continuous rather than saltatory propagation across a membrane no longer optimized for it.

histology.heading: Gray and White Matter Organization
points: Gray matter consists predominantly of neuronal cell bodies, dendrites, unmyelinated axon segments, and glial cells, and is the site of synaptic integration; in the spinal cord it forms a central butterfly-shaped region, while in the cerebrum and cerebellum it forms an outer cortical layer plus deep nuclei.

White matter consists predominantly of myelinated axon tracts (the myelin's lipid content giving it a pale, glistening appearance relative to gray matter) and functions primarily as a conduction pathway connecting different gray matter regions rather than a site of synaptic processing.

The isocortex (neocortex, comprising the great majority of the human cerebral cortex) is organized into six histological layers, from the outer molecular layer (largely axons and dendrites, few cell bodies) through layers containing progressively denser pyramidal and granule cell populations to the innermost layer bordering the white matter; the specific thickness and cellular composition of each layer varies by cortical region and function (e.g., primary motor cortex has a thinned granular layer IV and prominent pyramidal layer V, reflecting its output-heavy role; primary sensory cortices show the opposite emphasis).

histology.heading: Choroid Plexus and Meningeal Histology
points: The choroid plexus consists of a monolayer of specialized cuboidal epithelial cells (continuous with ventricular ependyma) resting on a basal lamina, enclosing a core of loose connective tissue and fenestrated capillaries; the apical (CSF-facing) surface bears dense microvilli, increasing surface area for the active secretory processes that generate CSF.

Tight junctions link adjacent choroid epithelial cells specifically at their apical (ventricular) pole — an arrangement that positions the blood-facing lateral intercellular spaces outside the barrier, distinct from the epithelial tight-junction arrangement typical of other secretory epithelia, and is thought to prevent osmotic gradients from driving fluid transport in the wrong direction.

The meninges — the three connective tissue layers enveloping the brain and spinal cord — consist of the outer dura mater (tough, fibrous, containing dural venous sinuses), the middle arachnoid mater (a thin, avascular layer whose 'barrier cells' are joined by tight junctions, forming part of the blood-CSF barrier system), and the inner pia mater (a delicate, highly vascular layer closely applied to the brain and spinal cord surface, following its every contour). The subarachnoid space, between arachnoid and pia, contains circulating CSF and the major cerebral blood vessels.

respiratory.name: Respiratory System
respiratory.summary: The airways and lungs that move air, exchange gases, and regulate acid-base balance through the elimination of carbon dioxide.

physiology.heading: Pulmonary Mechanics: Compliance, Surfactant, and the Law of Laplace
points: Inspiration is active: the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles contract, increasing thoracic volume and decreasing intrapleural and alveolar pressure below atmospheric pressure, drawing air in down the resulting pressure gradient (Boyle's law). Expiration at rest is passive, driven by elastic recoil of the lungs and relaxation of inspiratory muscles; forced expiration recruits internal intercostal and abdominal muscles.

Lung compliance (ΔV/ΔP) describes the ease of lung expansion per unit pressure change and is inversely related to elastance (elastic recoil, or stiffness). Compliance is determined by two factors: the elastic fiber content of lung tissue (collagen and elastin in the interalveolar septa, which also generate outward radial traction helping to keep alveoli open) and the surface tension of the fluid lining the alveoli.

Surface tension at the air-liquid interface inside each alveolus creates an inward collapsing force, formalized by the Law of Laplace: pressure required to keep a hollow sphere distended = 2T/r, where T is surface tension and r is alveolar radius. Because pressure rises as radius falls, smaller alveoli would — in the absence of surfactant — generate higher internal pressure than larger ones and tend to collapse and empty into neighboring larger alveoli, a destabilizing tendency.

Pulmonary surfactant, a phospholipid-rich mixture secreted by type II alveolar cells, disrupts this instability by lowering surface tension more effectively as alveolar radius decreases (since surfactant molecules become more concentrated as the alveolar surface area shrinks), roughly equalizing the effective pressure across differently-sized alveoli and preventing smaller alveoli from collapsing into larger ones. Surfactant deficiency (as in neonatal respiratory distress syndrome, since surfactant secretion typically begins around 24-28 weeks gestation) dramatically increases the pressure required to keep alveoli open and promotes widespread atelectasis.

The lung and chest wall together form a combined compliance system: the chest wall's own elastic recoil favors outward expansion, opposing the lung's inward elastic recoil; their combined balance establishes functional residual capacity (FRC), the volume remaining in the lungs after a passive, relaxed expiration.

physiology.heading: Airflow, Resistance, and Lung Volumes
points: Airway resistance follows the same physical principles as vascular resistance: flow = pressure gradient / resistance (Ohm's law analogy), and resistance itself is described by Poiseuille's law (resistance ∝ 1/radius⁴ for a given length and gas viscosity) — meaning airway caliber, particularly at the level of the medium-sized bronchi, is the dominant determinant of airflow resistance, and even modest bronchoconstriction produces a disproportionately large increase in resistance.

Tidal volume (~500 mL at rest), inspiratory and expiratory reserve volumes, and residual volume (air remaining after maximal forced expiration, which cannot be measured by simple spirometry since it can never be exhaled) together determine total lung capacity (~6 L in an average adult).

Intrapleural pressure remains negative relative to atmospheric pressure throughout the normal respiratory cycle — a consequence of the opposing elastic forces of lung (inward) and chest wall (outward) pulling apart on the thin pleural fluid layer between them — keeping the lungs mechanically coupled to the chest wall via this pleural seal; loss of this negative pressure (e.g., pneumothorax, where air enters the pleural space) allows the lung to collapse independently of chest wall movement.

physiology.heading: Gas Exchange by Diffusion
points: Gas exchange across the alveolar-capillary membrane occurs by simple diffusion, governed by Fick's law: diffusion rate is proportional to membrane surface area and the partial pressure gradient across it, and inversely proportional to membrane thickness. The large alveolar surface area (~70 m²) and extremely thin respiratory membrane (~0.5 micron, comprising alveolar epithelium, fused basement membranes, and capillary endothelium) together optimize diffusion efficiency, normally allowing near-complete equilibration of blood and alveolar gas partial pressures well before blood finishes transiting the pulmonary capillary.

physiology.heading: Oxygen Transport and the Oxyhemoglobin Dissociation Curve
points: Only about 2% of blood oxygen is carried dissolved directly in plasma; the remaining ~98% is bound to hemoglobin as oxyhemoglobin. Hemoglobin is a tetramer of four globin chains, each with a heme group whose central iron (Fe2+) reversibly binds one O2 molecule.

Hemoglobin exhibits cooperative (allosteric) oxygen binding: it shifts between a low-affinity 'tense' (T) conformation and a high-affinity 'relaxed' (R) conformation, and the binding of each successive O2 molecule increases the affinity for the next (heme-heme interaction). This cooperativity produces the characteristic sigmoidal shape of the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve — a flat upper plateau (where large changes in PO2 produce little change in saturation, providing a safety margin at high altitude or with mild lung disease) and a steep middle portion (where small changes in PO2 near typical tissue oxygen tensions produce large changes in O2 unloading).

The curve shifts rightward (reduced hemoglobin-oxygen affinity, favoring O2 unloading to tissues) with increased temperature, increased CO2, decreased pH, and increased 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG, a red blood cell metabolite that stabilizes the low-affinity T state) — the pH/CO2 dependence specifically termed the Bohr effect. These are all conditions characteristic of actively metabolizing tissue, meaning the curve's rightward shift is itself a physiological adaptation that promotes oxygen delivery exactly where and when it's most needed.

The curve shifts leftward (increased affinity, favoring O2 loading/retention) with fetal hemoglobin (alpha2gamma2, which binds 2,3-BPG less avidly than adult hemoglobin, allowing the fetus to extract oxygen from maternal circulation across the placenta) and with carbon monoxide poisoning (CO binds hemoglobin with roughly 240 times the affinity of O2, both directly displacing O2 and allosterically shifting remaining O2-bound sites toward tighter retention — compounding the harm of reduced oxygen-carrying capacity with impaired oxygen release from whatever hemoglobin remains available).

physiology.heading: Carbon Dioxide Transport
points: CO2 is transported in blood in three forms: dissolved in plasma (~10%), bound to hemoglobin as carbaminohemoglobin (~10%, binding the amino-terminus of the globin chain, a distinct site from oxygen binding), and — the majority, ~70% — as bicarbonate (HCO3-).

Bicarbonate formation occurs predominantly within red blood cells: CO2 diffuses into the erythrocyte and combines with water, catalyzed by carbonic anhydrase, to form carbonic acid, which rapidly dissociates into H+ and HCO3-. The H+ produced is buffered by hemoglobin (deoxygenated hemoglobin is a better H+ buffer than oxygenated hemoglobin, a property termed the Haldane effect, which reciprocally supports the Bohr effect at the tissue level), while HCO3- is exported from the cell into plasma in exchange for chloride via the Cl-/HCO3- antiporter (Band 3/anion exchanger 1) — the chloride shift, giving venous blood a higher bicarbonate and lower chloride concentration than arterial blood.

In the pulmonary capillaries, this entire process reverses: as CO2 diffuses out of the blood into the alveoli (down its partial pressure gradient) and is exhaled, chloride shift and carbonic anhydrase run in reverse, HCO3- re-enters red blood cells and is converted back to CO2 for elimination.

physiology.heading: Control of Breathing: Central and Peripheral Chemoreceptors
points: The medullary respiratory center (dorsal and ventral respiratory groups) generates the basic rhythm of breathing, modulated by the pontine respiratory group, which fine-tunes rate and depth; this rhythm is continuously adjusted by chemoreceptor feedback reflecting the body's current metabolic gas exchange needs.

Central chemoreceptors, located on the ventral surface of the medulla, are the dominant driver of ventilatory control under normal conditions, accounting for roughly 70-80% of the response to a rise in CO2. Because H+ itself cannot cross the blood-brain barrier, central chemoreceptors do not sense blood H+ directly — instead, CO2 (which crosses the BBB readily) diffuses into the CSF, where carbonic anhydrase converts it to carbonic acid, which dissociates and lowers CSF pH; this pH drop is what directly stimulates the chemoreceptors. Because CSF contains far less protein buffering capacity than blood, CSF pH changes more readily with fluctuating PCO2, making this an unusually sensitive detection system for even small changes in ventilation adequacy.

Peripheral chemoreceptors, located in the carotid bodies (at the common carotid bifurcation, signaling via the glossopharyngeal nerve) and aortic bodies (signaling via the vagus nerve), respond mainly to a fall in arterial PO2 — becoming significant drivers of ventilation only once PO2 drops substantially (roughly below 60 mmHg), since it is the partial pressure of dissolved oxygen, not total oxygen content, that constitutes the actual stimulus (explaining why conditions like anemia, which reduce oxygen content without lowering PO2, do not directly stimulate these receptors). Peripheral chemoreceptors also respond to rising CO2/falling pH, though more weakly and with a faster response time than central chemoreceptors, and account for roughly 15-20% of the overall ventilatory drive.

Because CO2/pH is the dominant physiological driver of ventilation, chronic CO2 retainers (e.g., in advanced COPD) were classically thought to become reliant on hypoxic drive via peripheral chemoreceptors as their central chemoreceptor sensitivity blunted — the traditional rationale for cautious oxygen administration in this population. More recent evidence indicates this mechanism is less significant than previously believed, and that excess supplemental oxygen instead risks worsening hypercapnia chiefly by reversing protective hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, worsening ventilation-perfusion mismatch.

physiology.heading: Ventilation-Perfusion Matching
points: Efficient gas exchange requires that ventilation (airflow to alveoli) and perfusion (blood flow to the surrounding capillaries) be appropriately matched at the regional level — expressed as the V/Q ratio, ideally close to 1 in a well-matched lung unit.

Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction is a unique, localized reflex in which pulmonary arterioles supplying poorly-ventilated (low-PO2) alveoli constrict, redirecting blood flow toward better-ventilated regions — the opposite response seen in the systemic circulation, where hypoxia causes vasodilation. This reflex actively optimizes overall V/Q matching by minimizing blood flow to lung units that could not adequately oxygenate it anyway.

Gravity produces substantial regional V/Q variation in the upright lung: at the apex, alveoli are relatively over-ventilated relative to their perfusion (high V/Q, since gravity limits blood flow reaching the apex more than it limits ventilation there), while at the base, alveoli are relatively over-perfused relative to their ventilation (low V/Q, since gravity increases blood flow preferentially more than it increases regional ventilation) — meaning gas exchange efficiency, and the relative contribution of different lung regions to overall oxygenation, varies continuously from apex to base.

histology.heading: Airway Epithelium
points: The trachea and bronchi are lined with pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with interspersed goblet cells, forming the mucociliary escalator that traps and clears inhaled debris — cilia beat in a coordinated, unidirectional wave, propelling the overlying mucus (and trapped particulates) toward the pharynx to be swallowed or expectorated.

C-shaped hyaline cartilage rings support the trachea, preventing collapse during the negative intrathoracic pressures of inspiration while allowing posterior flexibility against the adjacent esophagus during swallowing.

As airways branch progressively into bronchioles, the epithelium transitions from pseudostratified columnar to simple columnar and then simple cuboidal, while cartilage and goblet cells progressively disappear — reflecting the airway's shifting mechanical role (from structural conduit toward the highly branched, thin-walled distribution network feeding the alveoli) and the decreasing need for mucus production as inhaled particulates have typically already been filtered by more proximal airways.

Club cells (formerly termed Clara cells), found in the bronchiolar epithelium, secrete surfactant lipoprotein components, detoxify inhaled xenobiotics via cytochrome P450 enzymes, and act as regional progenitor cells capable of re-epithelializing the bronchiolar lining after injury, functionally replacing the goblet cells that are absent at this level.

histology.heading: Alveolar Structure
points: Type I pneumocytes are thin, flat squamous cells forming the large majority (~95%) of the alveolar surface area despite being outnumbered by type II cells; their extreme thinness is specifically optimized to minimize diffusion distance for gas exchange, and — having essentially no capacity for cell division — they are particularly vulnerable to toxic or infectious lung injury.

Type II pneumocytes are cuboidal, fewer in number but metabolically active, secreting pulmonary surfactant via lamellar bodies (specialized secretory organelles); they also serve as the stem/progenitor cell population responsible for regenerating both type I and type II cells following alveolar injury.

Alveolar macrophages ('dust cells') patrol the alveolar luminal surface, phagocytosing inhaled particulates, microorganisms, and cellular debris; unlike much of the mucociliary escalator's mechanical clearance, this defense operates at the level of the alveolus itself, where cilia and mucus are absent.

The respiratory membrane — the actual gas-exchange barrier between alveolar air and capillary blood — comprises the type I pneumocyte, a fused basement membrane shared between the alveolar epithelium and capillary endothelium, and the capillary endothelial cell itself; at roughly 0.5 microns thick in its thinnest regions, this multilayered barrier is nonetheless thin enough to permit near-complete gas equilibration during the brief transit time of a red blood cell through the pulmonary capillary.

histology.heading: Pleura
points: The lung is enveloped by visceral pleura (a single mesothelial layer adherent directly to the lung surface, following its every fissure and contour) and separated by a thin, potential pleural space from the parietal pleura (mesothelium lining the inner chest wall, diaphragm, and mediastinum).

The pleural space normally contains only a thin film of serous lubricating fluid, continuously produced and reabsorbed, allowing the visceral and parietal layers to glide smoothly against one another during breathing while the fluid's surface tension keeps the two layers mechanically coupled — the physical basis for the lung following chest wall movement despite having no direct structural attachment to it.

digestive.name: Digestive System
digestive.summary: The gastrointestinal tract and accessory organs that mechanically and chemically break down food, absorb nutrients, and eliminate waste.

physiology.heading: The Enteric Nervous System and GI Motility Pacemaking
points: The gastrointestinal tract is innervated by the enteric nervous system (ENS), a division of the peripheral nervous system capable of controlling motility and secretion largely independently of central input, though normally modulated by autonomic (sympathetic/parasympathetic) innervation. The ENS comprises two interconnected networks: the myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus, situated between the circular and longitudinal layers of the muscularis externa and primarily governing motility, and the submucosal (Meissner's) plexus, governing secretion and local blood flow.

Interstitial cells of Cajal (ICCs), specialized pacemaker cells interspersed between smooth muscle cells and enteric nerve endings throughout the GI tract, generate the rhythmic, spontaneous slow-wave electrical activity that underlies coordinated GI motility — analogous in concept to the SA node's role in the heart, though the GI tract's slow waves set the rhythm and frequency of contraction rather than directly causing it (an actual contraction still requires the slow wave to reach threshold, typically via superimposed neural or hormonal input).

Peristalsis — coordinated waves of muscular contraction propelling luminal contents distally — depends on coordinated activity between excitatory (acetylcholine, substance P) and inhibitory (nitric oxide, vasoactive intestinal peptide) myenteric motor neurons acting on the ICC network: contraction of the circular muscle behind the bolus and relaxation ahead of it, both propagating in a coordinated wave via gap-junction communication between myenteric neurons.

The migrating motor complex (MMC) is a distinct, cyclical pattern of motility occurring in the fasted (interdigestive) state, sweeping the stomach and small intestine clear of residual debris and bacteria in a series of phases (a quiescent period, an irregular period, and a brief but intense period of peak contractile activity) that migrate progressively from stomach to terminal ileum roughly every 90-120 minutes; the hormone motilin, released from the duodenum and jejunum, closely correlates with and helps drive the onset of the MMC's active phase.

physiology.heading: Gastric Acid Secretion
points: Gastric parietal cells secrete hydrochloric acid via the H+/K+-ATPase (proton pump), which actively exchanges cytoplasmic H+ for luminal K+ against a massive concentration gradient — gastric juice can reach a pH near 0.8-1, meaning luminal H+ concentration is roughly a million-fold higher than in blood plasma. In the resting state, this pump sits inactive within cytoplasmic tubulovesicles; upon stimulation, these vesicles fuse with the apical membrane, inserting active proton pumps into the canalicular surface.

Three convergent signals stimulate acid secretion, acting on distinct parietal cell receptors: acetylcholine (from vagal/enteric neurons, acting on muscarinic M3 receptors), gastrin (from antral G cells, acting on CCK2 receptors), and histamine (from neighboring enterochromaffin-like cells, acting on H2 receptors). Histamine's H2-receptor-mediated cAMP signaling is the dominant and rate-limiting pathway, which is why H2 blockers and proton pump inhibitors (targeting the final common pathway) are both effective acid-suppressing therapies, and why acetylcholine/gastrin also potentiate acid secretion partly by promoting local histamine release.

Acid secretion is classically divided into three overlapping phases: the cephalic phase (triggered by the sight, smell, taste, or thought of food, mediated via vagal output, accounting for a substantial fraction of total secretion before food even reaches the stomach), the gastric phase (triggered by gastric distension and the presence of peptides/amino acids, the largest contributor, mediated by both local reflexes and gastrin release), and the intestinal phase (initially stimulatory as chyme enters the duodenum, but rapidly becoming net inhibitory as acid, fat, and hypertonicity in the duodenum trigger feedback signals — including secretin and the enterogastric reflex — that suppress further gastric acid output and emptying).

During active acid secretion, bicarbonate generated intracellularly (from CO2 and water via carbonic anhydrase, alongside the H+ pumped into the lumen) exits the parietal cell across the basolateral membrane in exchange for chloride, producing a measurable rise in blood bicarbonate after a meal — the alkaline tide.

physiology.heading: Enzymatic Digestion of Macronutrients
points: Carbohydrate digestion begins with salivary amylase (starch), is interrupted by gastric acid (which denatures amylase), and resumes with pancreatic amylase in the duodenum, ultimately producing disaccharides that are cleaved by brush-border enzymes (maltase, sucrase, lactase) into absorbable monosaccharides.

Protein digestion begins with pepsin in the stomach (a protease active only at low pH, itself activated from pepsinogen by existing gastric acid — an autocatalytic activation loop), continues with pancreatic proteases secreted as inactive zymogens (trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen, procarboxypeptidase) that are sequentially activated in the duodenum — enteropeptidase (a brush-border enzyme) converts trypsinogen to active trypsin, which then activates the remaining pancreatic zymogens, including more trypsinogen (a further autocatalytic amplification) — and finishes with brush-border peptidases producing free amino acids and small peptides.

Fat digestion requires bile salts (amphipathic molecules synthesized in the liver from cholesterol, conjugated with glycine or taurine to increase water solubility) to emulsify large fat globules into an oil-in-water suspension, dramatically increasing the surface area available for pancreatic lipase (which requires a co-secreted protein cofactor, colipase, to function effectively at this lipid-water interface). Lipase products (free fatty acids, monoglycerides) then combine with bile salts and other lipid-soluble products to form micelles, which shuttle these otherwise water-insoluble products to the enterocyte brush border for absorption.

physiology.heading: Absorption Mechanisms
points: Villi and microvilli in the small intestine vastly amplify the absorptive surface area. Glucose and galactose are absorbed via SGLT1, a secondary active transporter on the apical enterocyte membrane that couples sugar uptake to the inward Na+ gradient established by basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase; fructose, lacking this Na+-coupling, instead enters via GLUT5 through facilitated diffusion. All three monosaccharides then exit the enterocyte's basolateral membrane via GLUT2, entering the bloodstream and ultimately reaching the hepatic portal circulation.

Amino acids and small peptides are absorbed by multiple apical transport systems, many Na+-coupled (secondary active transport, analogous to SGLT1); intracellular peptidases further hydrolyze absorbed oligopeptides to free amino acids before basolateral export into the interstitial space and portal circulation.

Long-chain fatty acids and monoglycerides, delivered to the enterocyte brush border within bile salt micelles, diffuse across the apical membrane (the bile salts themselves are left behind in the lumen for eventual reabsorption further downstream). Within the enterocyte, these products are re-esterified into triglycerides, packaged with cholesterol and apolipoproteins into chylomicrons, and — unlike sugars and amino acids — exported into lacteals (specialized lymphatic capillaries within each villus) rather than blood capillaries directly, since chylomicrons are too large to cross typical capillary endothelium.

Bile salts are not absorbed alongside the fats they helped digest; instead, they remain in the intestinal lumen throughout its length (maintaining a high luminal bile salt concentration to maximize ongoing lipid digestion) and are actively reabsorbed specifically at the terminal ileum via a Na+-coupled apical transporter. Reabsorbed bile salts return to the liver via the portal circulation for re-secretion — the enterohepatic circulation — with roughly 95% of the bile salt pool recycled this way per cycle and only a small fraction lost to fecal excretion (compensated by new hepatic synthesis).

physiology.heading: Hormonal Regulation of Digestion
points: Gastrin, secreted by antral G cells in response to gastric distension, luminal peptides/amino acids, and vagal stimulation, is the primary stimulus for gastric acid secretion and also promotes gastric motility and mucosal growth.

Secretin, secreted by duodenal S cells in response to acidic chyme entering the duodenum, stimulates pancreatic ductal cells to secrete bicarbonate-rich fluid, neutralizing gastric acid and creating the near-neutral pH environment pancreatic enzymes require for optimal activity; it also inhibits gastric acid secretion and motility, contributing to the intestinal phase's negative feedback on gastric emptying.

Cholecystokinin (CCK), secreted by duodenal I cells in response to luminal fats and amino acids, stimulates gallbladder contraction (releasing stored bile) and pancreatic acinar cell secretion of digestive enzymes, while also slowing gastric emptying and promoting satiety — coordinating enzyme/bile delivery with the actual presence of substrate requiring them.
Motilin, released cyclically from the duodenum during the fasted state, is the principal hormonal driver of the migrating motor complex's periodic housekeeping contractions.

histology.heading: General GI Wall Architecture
points: The GI tract wall, from esophagus to anal canal, follows a consistent four-layer plan: the mucosa (epithelium, lamina propria connective tissue, and a thin muscularis mucosae layer that independently allows local folding/movement of the mucosal surface), the submucosa (denser connective tissue containing larger blood vessels, lymphatics, and the submucosal plexus), the muscularis externa (typically an inner circular and outer longitudinal smooth muscle layer, with the myenteric plexus sandwiched between them), and the outermost serosa (in intraperitoneal segments) or adventitia (in retroperitoneal/extraperitoneal segments, lacking a mesothelial covering).

histology.heading: Regional Epithelial Specialization
points: The esophagus is lined with stratified squamous non-keratinized epithelium, providing resistance to the mechanical abrasion of swallowed food boluses — an epithelial type shared with other high-friction surfaces (the epidermis, by contrast, is keratinized, reflecting its additional need for a durable, desiccation-resistant outer barrier).

The stomach transitions to simple columnar epithelium, organized into gastric pits leading down to gastric glands whose cellular composition varies by region: the body/fundus glands contain parietal cells (HCl and intrinsic factor secretion, recognizable by their abundant mitochondria and characteristic intracellular canaliculi), chief cells (pepsinogen secretion, with basal rough ER and apical zymogen granules typical of a protein-secreting cell), and mucous neck cells; antral glands are comparatively richer in mucous and gastrin-secreting G cells.

The small intestine's simple columnar epithelium bears prominent microvilli (the ultrastructural basis of the light-microscopic 'brush border'), interspersed with mucus-secreting goblet cells (increasing in density distally, correlating with the shift from primarily absorptive duodenum/jejunum toward more mucus-dependent ileum) and, at the base of each crypt of Lieberkühn, Paneth cells (secreting antimicrobial peptides and lysozyme, helping regulate local microbial populations) alongside the intestinal stem cells responsible for continuously repopulating the rapidly-turning-over epithelium.

The large intestine's simple columnar epithelium has abundant goblet cells and straight, unbranched crypts, but — reflecting its role in water/electrolyte absorption and waste consolidation rather than nutrient absorption — lacks the villi present throughout the small intestine, giving its mucosal surface a comparatively flat appearance on cross-section.

histology.heading: Accessory Organ Histology
points: The liver's functional architecture is classically described in terms of the hepatic lobule: hexagonal units with a central vein at the center and portal triads (a bile ductule, hepatic artery branch, and portal vein branch, traveling together) at each of the six corners.
