Hepatocytes are arranged in single-cell-thick plates radiating outward from the central vein, with blood flowing from the portal triads through low-pressure sinusoids (lined by discontinuous, fenestrated endothelium permitting free exchange of plasma proteins) toward the central vein, while bile flows in the opposite direction — from hepatocytes into bile canaliculi and outward toward the portal bile ductules — an anatomically countercurrent arrangement relative to blood flow.

The exocrine pancreas consists of acinar cells (pyramidal, protein-secreting cells with basal rough ER and apical zymogen granules, closely resembling gastric chief cells structurally) arranged in grape-like clusters (acini) that drain via a branching ductal system into the main pancreatic duct; duct cells contribute the bicarbonate-rich fluid that neutralizes gastric acid entering the duodenum. The endocrine pancreas (islets of Langerhans) forms small, well-vascularized cell clusters scattered among the exocrine acinar tissue, distinguishable histologically by their comparatively pale-staining cytoplasm relative to the surrounding zymogen-rich acinar cells.

The gallbladder is lined by simple columnar epithelium with extensive apical microvilli, adapted for its function of concentrating stored bile by actively absorbing water and electrolytes; its wall lacks a submucosa and distinct muscularis mucosae, and its muscularis is composed of smooth muscle bundles running in multiple orientations (rather than the GI tract's typical distinct circular/longitudinal layering) to support efficient, omnidirectional contraction during gallbladder emptying.

renal.name: Renal System
renal.summary: The kidneys and urinary tract that filter blood, regulate fluid and electrolyte balance, and maintain acid-base homeostasis.

physiology.heading: Glomerular Filtration: Starling Forces and Determinants of GFR
points: The nephron is the functional unit of the kidney, each comprising a renal corpuscle (glomerulus plus Bowman's capsule) and a renal tubule; each kidney contains roughly one million nephrons. Glomerular filtration rate (GFR, normal ~120-125 mL/min) equals the filtration coefficient (Kf, reflecting membrane surface area and permeability) multiplied by net filtration pressure — itself the sum of four opposing Starling forces across the glomerular capillary wall.

Two forces favor filtration: glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure (PGC, unusually high — roughly 50 mmHg, about half of systemic arterial pressure, since blood arrives via a short, low-resistance afferent arteriole from the renal artery) and Bowman's capsule oncotic pressure (πBC, normally negligible, since the healthy filtration barrier excludes essentially all plasma protein). Two forces oppose filtration: Bowman's capsule hydrostatic pressure (PBC, generated by the resistance of downstream tubular flow) and glomerular capillary oncotic pressure (πGC, which rises progressively along the length of the glomerular capillary as water is filtered out and protein concentration in the remaining plasma correspondingly increases).

Glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure — and therefore GFR — is set by the relative resistances of the afferent and efferent arterioles: afferent arteriolar constriction reduces PGC (and GFR) by limiting inflow, while efferent arteriolar constriction paradoxically raises PGC (and, over a moderate range, GFR) by impeding outflow, though severe efferent constriction can eventually reduce GFR by excessively raising πGC and reducing renal plasma flow. This differential control allows physiological mechanisms (and pharmacological agents such as ACE inhibitors, which preferentially dilate the efferent arteriole) to influence GFR somewhat independently of overall renal blood flow.

Filtration fraction — the proportion of renal plasma flow actually filtered at the glomerulus, normally ~20% — links glomerular and peritubular capillary physiology: since roughly 20% of plasma water and virtually no protein leaves via filtration, the blood entering the peritubular capillaries downstream of the efferent arteriole is more concentrated (higher oncotic pressure) than typical systemic capillary blood, which is precisely what drives the oncotic-pressure-favored reabsorption of fluid from the proximal tubule interstitium back into the peritubular capillaries.

physiology.heading: Autoregulation of Renal Blood Flow and GFR
points: The kidney maintains remarkably stable renal blood flow and GFR across a wide range of systemic arterial pressures (roughly 80-180 mmHg) via two intrinsic autoregulatory mechanisms, protecting the filtration apparatus from pressure-driven damage while still permitting adequate excretion of metabolic waste.

The myogenic mechanism is the more rapid of the two: increased pressure stretches afferent arteriolar smooth muscle, triggering reflexive vascular smooth muscle contraction (stretch-activated Ca2+ channels increasing intracellular Ca2+) that constricts the vessel and limits the rise in downstream glomerular pressure; reduced pressure produces the mirror-image relaxation and dilation.

Tubuloglomerular feedback (TGF) operates via the juxtaglomerular apparatus, where specialized macula densa cells of the thick ascending limb — positioned adjacent to their own nephron's afferent arteriole — sense the NaCl concentration of tubular fluid passing by. A rise in GFR increases tubular flow rate, reducing the time available for NaCl reabsorption in upstream segments and thus increasing NaCl delivery to the macula densa; the macula densa responds by releasing vasoconstrictive mediators (including ATP/adenosine) acting on the adjacent afferent arteriole, constricting it and returning GFR toward normal — a negative feedback loop operating at the level of each individual nephron.

The two mechanisms are complementary in speed and stimulus: the myogenic response reacts within seconds to pressure changes directly, while tubuloglomerular feedback reacts somewhat more slowly to the downstream consequence of altered filtration (tubular NaCl delivery), together providing robust protection against both acute pressure surges and sustained filtration abnormalities.

physiology.heading: Tubular Reabsorption and Secretion Along the Nephron
points: The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs the bulk (roughly two-thirds) of filtered water, essentially all filtered glucose and amino acids (via multiple Na+-coupled secondary active transporters), and a proportional majority of filtered Na+, Cl-, and HCO3- — largely isosmotic reabsorption, meaning tubular fluid osmolarity remains essentially unchanged from the original filtrate despite the large volume reabsorbed.

The thin descending limb of the loop of Henle is highly water-permeable (via abundant AQP1 channels) but relatively impermeable to solutes, so as tubular fluid descends into the progressively hyperosmotic medullary interstitium, water passively exits until the tubular fluid approaches osmotic equilibrium with its surroundings, concentrating the remaining solutes.

The thick ascending limb, conversely, is essentially impermeable to water but actively reabsorbs NaCl via the apical Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter (NKCC2, the molecular target of loop diuretics such as furosemide) — since solute leaves without accompanying water, tubular fluid becomes progressively more dilute as it ascends, while the reabsorbed NaCl contributes directly to building the surrounding medullary hyperosmotic gradient.

The distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct perform fine, hormonally-regulated adjustment of final urine composition: aldosterone-sensitive principal cells reabsorb Na+ (via ENaC channels) and secrete K+, while the collecting duct's water permeability is set almost entirely by circulating ADH (via aquaporin-2 channel insertion), allowing final urine osmolarity to be adjusted across an enormous range (as dilute as ~50 mOsm/L or as concentrated as ~1200-1400 mOsm/L) according to the body's current hydration status.

physiology.heading: Countercurrent Multiplication and the Medullary Concentration Gradient
points: The kidney's capacity to produce urine far more concentrated than plasma depends on the countercurrent multiplier system formed by the loop of Henle. Because the descending and ascending limbs run adjacent to one another with fluid flowing in opposite directions, and because the ascending limb actively pumps NaCl out (while remaining impermeable to water) while the descending limb passively loses water (while remaining largely impermeable to solute), a progressively increasing osmotic gradient is established from the corticomedullary junction (~300 mOsm/L, isosmotic with plasma) down to the tip of the deepest loops in the inner medulla (~1200 mOsm/L in humans) — small individual transverse gradients between the two limbs are 'multiplied' along the length of the loop into a much larger longitudinal gradient.

Urea contributes substantially (roughly half) to the inner medullary osmotic gradient through a recycling process: urea is concentrated in the collecting duct as water is reabsorbed under ADH's influence, then — since the inner medullary collecting duct becomes urea-permeable under ADH stimulation — diffuses into the medullary interstitium, from which some re-enters the thin limbs of the loop of Henle and is carried back toward the collecting duct, progressively trapping and concentrating urea deep in the medulla independent of active NaCl transport.

The vasa recta — specialized peritubular capillaries running parallel to the loop of Henle — preserve rather than create this gradient, functioning as a passive countercurrent exchanger rather than a multiplier: as blood descends into the hyperosmotic medulla it passively loses water and gains solute (equilibrating with the interstitium), and as it ascends back toward the cortex it passively regains water and loses solute, meaning blood delivers oxygen and nutrients to medullary tissue without washing away the osmotic gradient the loop of Henle worked to establish.

physiology.heading: Hormonal Regulation of Fluid and Electrolyte Balance
points: The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) is triggered by reduced renal perfusion pressure (sensed by afferent arteriolar baroreceptors), reduced NaCl delivery to the macula densa, or direct beta-1 adrenergic stimulation of juxtaglomerular cells — all converging to trigger renin release, initiating the angiotensin II/aldosterone cascade that increases distal nephron Na+ (and secondary water) reabsorption, expanding plasma volume and raising blood pressure.

Antidiuretic hormone (ADH/vasopressin), synthesized by hypothalamic neurons and released from the posterior pituitary in response to rising plasma osmolarity (sensed by hypothalamic osmoreceptors) or significant volume depletion, increases aquaporin-2 channel insertion into the apical membrane of collecting duct principal cells, increasing water reabsorption and concentrating urine — its collecting-duct target is precisely the segment where the medullary gradient established by countercurrent multiplication can be exploited to draw water out of the tubule.

Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP), released by atrial myocytes in response to stretch from elevated blood volume, opposes RAAS: it promotes both natriuresis (increased Na+ excretion, partly via afferent arteriolar dilation increasing GFR and directly inhibiting distal Na+ reabsorption) and diuresis, and also suppresses renin and aldosterone release — an integrated counter-regulatory response to volume overload.

physiology.heading: Renal Regulation of Acid-Base Balance
points: The kidneys complement the lungs' rapid CO2-based respiratory compensation with slower (hours to days) but more complete acid-base regulation, achieved through two parallel processes: reclaiming virtually all filtered bicarbonate (preventing its loss, which would otherwise represent a major daily base loss) and generating new bicarbonate to replace that consumed buffering the body's ongoing metabolic acid production.

Filtered bicarbonate reabsorption occurs predominantly in the proximal tubule (~85-90%) via an indirect mechanism: apical Na+/H+ exchange (NHE3) secretes H+ into the lumen, where it combines with filtered HCO3- to form carbonic acid, which luminal carbonic anhydrase rapidly converts to CO2 and water; CO2 freely diffuses into the tubular cell, where intracellular carbonic anhydrase reverses the reaction, regenerating H+ (recycled for further NHE3 exchange) and HCO3- (exported across the basolateral membrane into blood via a Na+-HCO3- cotransporter) — the net effect is bicarbonate reabsorption without the originally-filtered bicarbonate ion itself ever crossing the tubular cell.

New bicarbonate generation — necessary to replace the bicarbonate consumed neutralizing the roughly 1 mEq/kg/day of fixed (non-volatile) acid produced by normal metabolism — occurs via two mechanisms: titratable acid excretion (filtered buffers, chiefly phosphate, accepting secreted H+ in the tubular lumen and being excreted as such, with each H+ buffered corresponding to one new HCO3- generated and returned to blood) and ammoniagenesis, the more important and more adjustable of the two.

In renal ammoniagenesis, proximal tubule cells metabolize glutamine to glutamate and ammonium (NH4+), a process that simultaneously generates new bicarbonate (via further metabolism of the resulting carbon skeleton to bicarbonate, exported basolaterally into blood); the ammonium is secreted into the tubular lumen (via apical NHE3, substituting NH4+ for H+), largely reabsorbed in the thick ascending limb, recycled through the medullary interstitium, and ultimately re-secreted as NH3 by the collecting duct, where it combines with H+ secreted by intercalated cells to re-form NH4+, which — being charged and thus unable to diffuse back across the tubular membrane — becomes trapped in the lumen and excreted, permanently removing that hydrogen ion (and equivalent generated bicarbonate) from the body. Ammoniagenesis is markedly upregulated during systemic acidosis, making it the kidney's primary adjustable lever for increasing net acid excretion.

The collecting duct additionally contains two functionally distinct intercalated cell populations that fine-tune final urinary acid-base handling: type A intercalated cells secrete H+ via an apical H+-ATPase (reclaiming bicarbonate basolaterally), active during acidosis, while type B intercalated cells run the opposite arrangement — a basolateral H+-ATPase and an apical Cl-/HCO3- exchanger (pendrin) that secretes bicarbonate into urine — active during alkalosis. This bidirectional cellular capability allows the distal nephron to independently fine-tune net acid or base excretion according to the body's current systemic acid-base status.

histology.heading: Renal Corpuscle Histology
points: The glomerulus is a specialized capillary tuft with fenestrated endothelium (large pores, though — unlike most fenestrated capillaries elsewhere — lacking diaphragms across the fenestrae, permitting free passage of water and small solutes while excluding cells), surrounded by Bowman's capsule. The visceral layer of Bowman's capsule is formed by podocytes, whose primary processes extend into numerous secondary foot processes (pedicels) that interdigitate with those of neighboring podocytes, leaving narrow filtration slits bridged by a slit diaphragm — together with the underlying fused glomerular basement membrane, forming the size- and charge-selective filtration barrier.

Mesangial cells, located between glomerular capillary loops, provide structural support, exhibit contractile properties that can regulate glomerular capillary surface area (and thus Kf), and phagocytose trapped macromolecular debris from the filtration process.

histology.heading: Tubular Segment Histology
points: The proximal tubule is lined by simple cuboidal epithelium bearing a prominent apical brush border (dense microvilli, visible by light microscopy as an eosinophilic fringe), which vastly increases the luminal surface area available for the massive reabsorptive workload of this segment; cells are packed with mitochondria and exhibit extensive basolateral membrane infolding, both reflecting the high demand for active transport.

The thin segments of the loop of Henle (thin descending and, in long-looped nephrons, thin ascending limb) are lined by simple squamous epithelium with few organelles, consistent with their role in passive rather than active transport.

The thick ascending limb transitions back to simple cuboidal epithelium, again with extensive basolateral infolding and abundant mitochondria housing the Na+/K+-ATPase that powers active NaCl reabsorption via NKCC2.

The distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct are lined by simple cuboidal epithelium; the collecting duct specifically contains two functionally and histologically distinct cell populations — principal cells (paler cytoplasm, expressing ENaC and aquaporin channels, the primary site of aldosterone and ADH action) and intercalated cells (fewer, more densely staining due to abundant mitochondria, mediating acid-base transport as described above).

histology.heading: Cortex, Medulla, and Juxtaglomerular Apparatus
points: The renal cortex contains all renal corpuscles along with the proximal and distal convoluted tubule segments; the medulla, organized into cone-shaped renal pyramids, contains the loops of Henle and collecting ducts as they course toward the renal papilla.

The juxtaglomerular apparatus, situated at the vascular pole of each glomerulus where the thick ascending limb passes close to its own nephron's afferent (and efferent) arteriole, comprises three cell types: macula densa cells (specialized, closely-packed thick ascending limb epithelial cells sensing tubular NaCl concentration), juxtaglomerular (granular) cells (modified smooth muscle cells in the afferent arteriolar wall, storing and releasing renin), and extraglomerular mesangial cells (lacis cells, thought to relay signals between the macula densa and the arterioles) — together forming the structural substrate for tubuloglomerular feedback and RAAS activation.

skeletal.name: Skeletal System
skeletal.summary: The bones, cartilage, and joints that provide structural support, enable movement, protect internal organs, and regulate mineral homeostasis.

physiology.heading: Bone Remodeling: The RANKL/RANK/OPG Pathway
points: Bone is continuously remodeled throughout life via tightly coupled cycles of osteoclastic resorption followed by osteoblastic formation, occurring within discrete bone remodeling compartments — a process that repairs microdamage, allows adaptation to mechanical loading, and provides a mechanism for regulating blood calcium levels.

Osteoclast differentiation and activation are governed by the RANKL/RANK/OPG signaling axis: osteoblasts (and osteocytes) express RANKL (receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa-B ligand) on their surface, which binds RANK receptors on osteoclast precursor cells (derived from the monocyte/macrophage hematopoietic lineage), driving their differentiation into mature, bone-resorbing osteoclasts. Osteoblasts simultaneously secrete osteoprotegerin (OPG), a soluble decoy receptor that binds RANKL and prevents it from engaging RANK — meaning the ratio of RANKL to OPG produced by osteoblasts is the central determinant of local osteoclast activity and bone resorption rate.

Numerous systemic and local factors regulate bone turnover by shifting this RANKL/OPG ratio: parathyroid hormone increases RANKL and decreases OPG production (promoting resorption), while estrogen suppresses RANKL and osteoclast survival (explaining the sharp increase in bone turnover following the postmenopausal drop in estrogen). Glucocorticoids similarly increase RANKL and decrease OPG while directly promoting osteoblast apoptosis — a combination that explains the significant bone loss associated with chronic glucocorticoid therapy.

Osteocytes — former osteoblasts that become entombed within the mineralized matrix during bone formation, comprising over 90% of all bone cells — are now recognized as the primary mechanosensory cells of bone. Embedded within lacunae and interconnected via an extensive canalicular network, osteocytes detect mechanical strain (partly via strain-induced fluid flow through the canalicular system) and respond by adjusting their own RANKL and sclerostin production, directly linking local mechanical loading to local remodeling activity — the cellular basis of Wolff's law, whereby bone architecture adapts to habitual mechanical stress, strengthening along lines of load and undergoing resorption with disuse.

physiology.heading: The Parathyroid Hormone-Vitamin D Axis and Calcium Homeostasis
points: Serum calcium is tightly regulated (normal range roughly 8.5-10.5 mg/dL) via the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR), a G-protein-coupled receptor on parathyroid chief cells that continuously monitors extracellular ionized calcium concentration. Falling calcium reduces CaSR activation, which — counterintuitively for a typical negative-feedback receptor — disinhibits PTH release (i.e., low calcium promotes PTH secretion, while high calcium binding CaSR suppresses it).

PTH raises blood calcium through three coordinated actions across three organ systems. In bone, PTH increases the RANKL/OPG ratio (as above), promoting osteoclastic resorption and liberating both calcium and phosphate into the bloodstream — though this skeletal effect develops over hours to days, slower than PTH's renal actions. In the kidney, PTH acts rapidly (within minutes) to increase distal tubular calcium reabsorption (via upregulation of the TRPV5 calcium channel) while simultaneously decreasing proximal tubular phosphate reabsorption — a dual action that raises serum calcium while lowering serum phosphate, preventing the calcium-phosphate product from rising high enough to risk soft-tissue calcification.

PTH's third, indirect action is on the intestine: PTH has no direct intestinal receptor effect, but stimulates renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase, the enzyme converting inactive 25-hydroxyvitamin D to active calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D); calcitriol then acts on intestinal epithelium to increase active calcium (and phosphate) absorption, roughly 70-80% of which occurs in the ileum. This makes vitamin D activation itself PTH-dependent, and explains why PTH's full calcium-raising effect, though initiated rapidly at the kidney, only reaches its maximum over several hours as calcitriol synthesis and intestinal absorption ramp up.

Calcitonin, secreted by thyroid parafollicular (C) cells in response to hypercalcemia, opposes PTH by inhibiting osteoclast activity and modestly increasing renal calcium excretion — though its physiological role in adult human calcium homeostasis is considered comparatively minor relative to the dominant PTH-vitamin D axis, evidenced by the absence of significant calcium derangement in patients who have undergone total thyroidectomy (and thus lack calcitonin production).

physiology.heading: Endochondral Ossification and Longitudinal Bone Growth
points: Most bones of the body (excluding the flat bones of the skull and clavicle, which form via intramembranous ossification directly within mesenchymal tissue) develop through endochondral ossification: a hyaline cartilage template is progressively replaced by bone, beginning with a primary ossification center in the diaphysis (shaft) during fetal development and a secondary ossification center in each epiphysis (end) typically after birth.

Longitudinal bone growth after birth occurs at the epiphyseal (growth) plate, a persisting band of cartilage between epiphysis and diaphysis, organized into sequential functional zones: the resting zone (small, relatively inactive chondrocytes serving as a stem-cell-like reserve, secreting factors that orient the columns of proliferating cells below), the proliferative zone (chondrocytes arranged in columns parallel to the bone's long axis, undergoing rapid mitosis under growth hormone/IGF-1 influence — the zone primarily responsible for the actual increase in bone length), the hypertrophic zone (chondrocytes stop dividing and dramatically enlarge, accumulating glycogen and alkaline phosphatase in preparation for matrix calcification), and the zone of calcification/ossification (the hypertrophic cartilage matrix mineralizes, hypertrophic chondrocytes undergo apoptosis, and invading osteoblasts deposit new bone matrix on the calcified cartilage remnants, which are continuously remodeled into mature bone).

This growth process continues until the growth plate itself is eventually replaced by bone (epiphyseal closure/fusion, driven by rising sex steroid levels during puberty — explaining why growth plates close earlier in individuals with earlier puberty), after which further longitudinal growth is no longer possible; bone width, by contrast, can continue to increase throughout life via appositional growth, as osteoblasts in the periosteum deposit new bone on the external surface while osteoclasts resorb bone from the internal (endosteal) surface, jointly widening the medullary cavity to keep the bone's weight proportional to its increasing diameter.

physiology.heading: Joint Biomechanics
points: Synovial joints (e.g., knee, shoulder, hip) are freely movable and enclosed by a fibrous joint capsule lined internally by a synovial membrane, which secretes synovial fluid — a viscous, hyaluronic acid-rich filtrate of plasma that lubricates the joint, nourishes the avascular articular cartilage via diffusion, and provides shock absorption. Articular (hyaline) cartilage covering the bone surfaces provides an extremely low-friction interface (coefficient of friction lower than most engineered lubricated bearings) but has minimal intrinsic capacity for self-repair, since mature cartilage is avascular, aneural, and contains a sparse chondrocyte population with limited proliferative capacity.

Cartilaginous joints (e.g., the intervertebral discs, pubic symphysis) permit limited movement through the compressibility of interposed cartilage, while fibrous joints (e.g., cranial sutures) permit minimal to no movement, their bones united by dense fibrous connective tissue. Ligaments (connecting bone to bone) and tendons (connecting muscle to bone) are both composed of dense regular connective tissue with highly aligned collagen fibers, providing substantial tensile strength along the axis of habitual loading while retaining a degree of elasticity that helps absorb sudden mechanical loads.

histology.heading: Compact Bone: The Osteon (Haversian System)
points: Compact (cortical) bone is organized into osteons: cylindrical structural units consisting of concentric rings (lamellae) of mineralized bone matrix arranged around a central Haversian canal, which houses blood vessels and nerve fibers running roughly parallel to the bone's long axis. Perpendicular Volkmann's (perforating) canals interconnect adjacent Haversian canals, distributing the vascular supply across the full thickness of compact bone.

Each osteon is bounded by a cement line — a thin layer of matrix, low in collagen, that marks the outer limit of a given remodeling episode and is thought to help arrest the propagation of microcracks by deflecting them along the osteon boundary rather than allowing continued growth through adjacent, mechanically distinct osteons.

Osteocytes occupy lacunae between adjacent lamellae, with fine cytoplasmic processes extending through canaliculi (small radiating channels within the matrix) to contact neighboring osteocytes via gap junctions, forming an extensive interconnected network that supports both nutrient/waste exchange through the otherwise impermeable mineralized matrix and the mechanosensory signaling described in bone remodeling physiology above.

histology.heading: Bone Cell Types
points: Osteoprogenitor cells, derived from mesenchymal stem cells, reside in the periosteum and endosteum and serve as the proliferative reserve population from which osteoblasts are generated as needed for bone formation or repair.

Osteoblasts are cuboidal, matrix-synthesizing cells lining bone surfaces, secreting osteoid (unmineralized collagen-rich matrix) that subsequently mineralizes with calcium hydroxyapatite; following completion of matrix deposition, an individual osteoblast follows one of three fates — becoming a quiescent bone-lining cell, undergoing apoptosis, or becoming entombed within the matrix it just deposited to become an osteocyte.

Osteoclasts are large, multinucleated cells of hematopoietic (monocyte/macrophage lineage) origin, formed by fusion of multiple mononuclear precursors under RANKL stimulation; they resorb bone by sealing a region of matrix (forming a ruffled border and a specialized acidic microenvironment beneath, the Howship's lacuna) and secreting both acid (dissolving the mineral component) and proteolytic enzymes such as cathepsin K (degrading the organic collagen matrix).

histology.heading: Bone Architecture and Cartilage Types
points: Spongy (trabecular/cancellous) bone lacks the discrete cylindrical osteons of compact bone, instead forming an open lattice of interconnected trabeculae oriented along the bone's principal lines of mechanical stress, with adjacent marrow spaces filling the interstitial gaps; this architecture provides substantial strength relative to its mass, favoring locations (vertebral bodies, epiphyses of long bones) where weight reduction is advantageous without sacrificing load-bearing capacity.

Hyaline cartilage (found at articular surfaces, costal cartilage, and forming the fetal skeletal template/growth plate) has a glassy, relatively homogeneous matrix rich in type II collagen and proteoglycans, providing smooth, compression-resistant surfaces.

Fibrocartilage (found in intervertebral discs and menisci) contains dense bundles of type I collagen interspersed with chondrocytes, combining substantial tensile strength with compressive resistance — an intermediate structural profile between hyaline cartilage and dense connective tissue.
Elastic cartilage (found in the external ear and epiglottis) contains an abundance of elastic fibers in addition to its collagen matrix, providing the flexibility and recoil these structures require.

muscular.name: Muscular System
muscular.summary: The skeletal, cardiac, and smooth muscle tissues that generate force for movement, posture, and the function of hollow organs.

physiology.heading: The Neuromuscular Junction
points: The neuromuscular junction (NMJ) is the specialized synapse between a motor neuron and a skeletal muscle fiber; each mature skeletal muscle fiber is innervated by a single motor nerve terminal, which docks not by penetrating the muscle membrane but by fitting into deep sarcolemmal invaginations called junctional folds, densely packed with nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at their crests.

An arriving presynaptic action potential opens voltage-gated (P/Q-type) Ca2+ channels concentrated at the nerve terminal's active zones, and the resulting Ca2+ influx triggers fusion of acetylcholine-containing synaptic vesicles with the presynaptic membrane; each vesicle contains roughly 5,000-10,000 acetylcholine molecules (a 'quantum'), and even at rest, spontaneous single-vesicle release produces tiny miniature end-plate potentials, providing a baseline readout of NMJ integrity.

Released acetylcholine crosses the roughly 50 nm synaptic cleft and binds nicotinic receptors on the motor end plate, opening ligand-gated cation channels that shift the local membrane potential from around -90 mV toward roughly -45 mV — generating the end-plate potential (EPP). Unlike graded postsynaptic potentials in central synapses, a normal EPP is always well above threshold, reliably triggering a full muscle fiber action potential that then propagates along the sarcolemma and into the T-tubule system.

Acetylcholinesterase, concentrated within the synaptic cleft, rapidly hydrolyzes acetylcholine, ensuring each nerve impulse produces a single, precisely timed muscle response rather than sustained receptor activation — the pharmacological target of both therapeutic (pyridostigmine, for myasthenia gravis) and toxic (organophosphate) acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, which produce sustained depolarization and eventual neuromuscular blockade through receptor desensitization.

physiology.heading: Excitation-Contraction Coupling
points: Depolarization spreading along the T-tubules (transverse invaginations of the sarcolemma positioned at the A-I band junction in skeletal muscle) triggers a conformational change in dihydropyridine receptors (voltage sensors embedded in the T-tubule membrane); because these are mechanically coupled to adjacent ryanodine receptors on the sarcoplasmic reticulum (forming the triad junction, distinct from cardiac muscle's diad arrangement), this conformational change directly opens the ryanodine receptor channel without requiring a trigger calcium current — a purely mechanical (rather than calcium-induced) coupling mechanism unique to skeletal muscle.

Ca2+ released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum binds troponin C on the thin filament; this binding is cooperative — each Ca2+ ion bound increases the affinity of troponin C for the next, up to four Ca2+ ions per troponin C complex — producing a steep, switch-like relationship between rising cytosolic Ca2+ and the fraction of thin filament sites made available for contraction, rather than a gradual one.

Ca2+ binding causes a conformational shift in the troponin complex that displaces tropomyosin away from the myosin-binding sites on actin, exposing them for cross-bridge formation. Relaxation requires cytosolic Ca2+ to fall, driven by the SERCA (sarco/endoplasmic reticulum Ca2+-ATPase) pump actively returning Ca2+ to the sarcoplasmic reticulum; within the SR, the Ca2+-binding protein calsequestrin buffers free Ca2+ concentration, reducing the concentration gradient SERCA must pump against and thereby lowering the pump's overall workload.

physiology.heading: The Cross-Bridge Cycle
points: With myosin-binding sites exposed, the cross-bridge cycle proceeds through a defined sequence: starting from the rigor state (myosin bound to actin with no nucleotide present — the state responsible for rigor mortis once ATP synthesis ceases after death), ATP binding to the myosin head causes myosin to detach from actin, breaking the cross-bridge.

ATP hydrolysis to ADP and inorganic phosphate (Pi) causes the myosin head to change conformation, 're-cocking' into a high-energy position and advancing toward a new binding site further along the actin filament (without yet generating force, since the head is not yet attached). Myosin then rebinds actin at this new site, forming a fresh cross-bridge.

Release of the inorganic phosphate triggers the power stroke — the myosin head pivots, pulling the actin filament toward the sarcomere's center and generating the force of contraction — followed by ADP release, which returns myosin to the rigor state, bound tightly to actin, ready to repeat the cycle once new ATP binds. Each cycle advances the thin filament only a small increment, so sustained contraction requires many rapid, repeated cross-bridge cycles across the many myosin heads of each thick filament, continuing for as long as Ca2+ remains bound to troponin C and ATP remains available.

physiology.heading: Motor Unit Recruitment and Force Grading
points: A motor unit comprises a single motor neuron and every muscle fiber it innervates; because all fibers within one motor unit contract together in an all-or-nothing fashion whenever their neuron fires, whole-muscle force is graded not by varying individual fiber force but by two mechanisms: recruiting additional motor units, and adjusting each active unit's firing frequency (rate coding).

Motor unit recruitment follows Henneman's size principle: motor neurons are recruited in strict order from smallest to largest, because smaller motor neurons have higher input resistance and therefore reach firing threshold with less synaptic excitation than larger neurons. Since motor neuron size correlates closely with the number (and typically the fatigue-resistance) of muscle fibers they innervate, this ordering means the smallest, most fatigue-resistant motor units are recruited first for fine, low-force tasks, with progressively larger, more powerful (but more fatigable) units recruited only as greater force is demanded — an efficient strategy that reserves the most fatigable resources for when they are truly needed.

Rate coding complements recruitment: within an already-active motor unit, increasing the motor neuron's firing frequency causes successive twitches to summate (since a new contractile response can be triggered before the previous one has fully relaxed), producing progressively greater sustained force up to a smooth, fused tetanic contraction at sufficiently high firing rates.

physiology.heading: Muscle Fiber Types and Metabolism
points: Type I (slow-twitch, oxidative) fibers express a myosin heavy chain isoform with relatively low ATPase activity (slow cross-bridge cycling), are rich in mitochondria and myoglobin (giving them a characteristic dark red color), rely predominantly on oxidative phosphorylation, and are highly fatigue-resistant — suited to sustained, low-intensity activity such as postural maintenance.

Type IIx (fast-twitch, glycolytic) fibers express a myosin isoform with high ATPase activity (rapid cross-bridge cycling, generating high force and velocity quickly), rely predominantly on anaerobic glycolysis, contain comparatively few mitochondria, and fatigue rapidly — suited to brief, high-intensity efforts.

Type IIa fibers represent an intermediate profile: fast cross-bridge cycling combined with substantial oxidative capacity, offering a compromise between speed/force and fatigue resistance. Muscle fiber type composition within a given muscle is influenced by both genetics and training — endurance training tends to shift fiber metabolic properties toward a more oxidative profile, while resistance/sprint training favors glycolytic characteristics, though the extent to which fibers can convert between major types remains an area of ongoing research.

physiology.heading: The Length-Tension Relationship
points: Isometric force generation varies with sarcomere length according to the degree of overlap between thick and thin filaments: at an optimal resting length, the maximum possible number of myosin heads can form cross-bridges with actin, producing peak force. At shorter lengths, thin filaments from opposite ends of the sarcomere begin to overlap each other (interfering with effective cross-bridge formation) and the thick filament may abut the Z-discs, both reducing force output; at longer lengths, progressively less thick-thin filament overlap leaves fewer myosin heads within reach of actin, again reducing force.

This length-tension relationship has direct physiological relevance: it partly explains why joint angle affects maximal force output during resistance exercise (since joint angle determines muscle length and thus sarcomere length), and — at the whole-organ level — is conceptually analogous to (though mechanistically distinct in its molecular basis from) the length-dependent activation underlying the cardiac Frank-Starling mechanism.

histology.heading: Skeletal Muscle Structure
points: Skeletal muscle fibers are long, cylindrical, multinucleated cells formed during development by the fusion of many individual myoblasts; their nuclei are characteristically located peripherally, just beneath the sarcolemma, leaving the central cytoplasm free for the densely packed contractile apparatus.

Each fiber contains hundreds to thousands of myofibrils, threadlike bundles running the length of the cell, each composed of a linear series of repeating sarcomeres — the fundamental contractile unit, bounded at each end by a Z-disc and containing the interdigitating thick and thin filaments responsible for the fiber's cross-striated appearance under light microscopy.

Muscle tissue is organized hierarchically with nested connective tissue wrappings: individual fibers are surrounded by endomysium (fine reticular connective tissue, also housing the capillary network supplying each fiber); groups of fibers are bundled into fascicles wrapped in perimysium (denser connective tissue, also carrying larger blood vessels and nerve branches); and the whole muscle is enveloped by epimysium, continuous with the deep fascia and, ultimately, the tendon.

histology.heading: The Sarcomere in Detail
points: The A-band represents the full length of the thick (myosin) filaments and remains constant in length regardless of contraction state, since it reflects filament length rather than the degree of overlap. The I-band contains only thin (actin) filaments (not overlapped by thick filaments) and shortens as the sarcomere contracts, since increasing thick-thin filament overlap progressively encroaches on this zone. The H-zone, the central region of the A-band containing only thick filaments (not yet overlapped by thin filaments extending in from either side), also shortens with contraction and can disappear entirely at very short sarcomere lengths.

The Z-disc, a dense protein lattice (principally alpha-actinin) at each end of the sarcomere, anchors the thin filaments and serves as the structural boundary defining one sarcomere from the next; the M-line, at the sarcomere's center, similarly anchors and cross-links the thick filaments, stabilizing their precise hexagonal lateral spacing relative to one another.

histology.heading: Smooth and Cardiac Muscle Compared to Skeletal Muscle
points: Smooth muscle contains the same actin and myosin proteins as striated muscle but lacks the regular sarcomeric organization (and therefore the troponin complex and visible cross-striations) of skeletal and cardiac muscle; its thin and thick filaments are instead anchored to dense bodies scattered through the cytoplasm and attached to the cell membrane, arranged somewhat obliquely so that contraction produces a corkscrew-like shortening of the whole spindle-shaped, uninucleated cell. Because smooth muscle lacks troponin, its calcium-dependent regulation instead operates through calmodulin and myosin light-chain kinase, a fundamentally different molecular switch from the troponin-tropomyosin system of striated muscle.

Cardiac muscle retains the sarcomeric organization and cross-striations of skeletal muscle (and uses the same troponin-based regulatory mechanism) but consists of shorter, branching, typically uninucleated or binucleated cells joined end-to-end at intercalated discs, whose gap junctions allow direct electrical coupling between cells — a feature entirely absent from skeletal muscle, where each fiber is electrically independent and contracts only in direct response to its own individual neuromuscular junction input.

endocrine.name: Endocrine System
endocrine.summary: The glands and hormones that regulate metabolism, growth, stress response, and homeostasis through chemical signaling.

physiology.heading: Principles of Hormone Action and Signal Transduction
points: Hormones are chemical messengers secreted directly into the bloodstream, acting on distant target cells bearing specific receptors — distinguishing true endocrine signaling from paracrine (acting on neighboring cells) and autocrine (acting on the secreting cell itself) signaling, though the underlying receptor mechanisms are often shared across all three modes.

Lipid-soluble hormones (steroids, thyroid hormone) diffuse freely across the plasma membrane and bind intracellular or nuclear receptors, which — once hormone-bound — act directly as transcription factors, altering gene expression over a relatively slow timescale (hours) but producing effects that persist long after the hormone itself has cleared, since new protein synthesis must occur and be degraded before the effect ends. Because these hormones are largely water-insoluble, most circulate bound to plasma carrier proteins (e.g., thyroxine-binding globulin, cortisol-binding globulin), with only the small free/unbound fraction biologically active — a reservoir that buffers against rapid fluctuations in total hormone level.

Water-soluble hormones (peptides, catecholamines) cannot cross the plasma membrane and instead bind cell-surface receptors, triggering intracellular second-messenger cascades — G-protein-coupled receptors activating cyclic AMP, IP3/diacylglycerol, or other pathways, or receptor tyrosine kinases (as for insulin) directly phosphorylating downstream signaling proteins. These mechanisms produce more rapid onset (seconds to minutes) but generally shorter-duration effects than nuclear receptor signaling, since they act by modifying existing proteins (activity, localization) rather than requiring new gene transcription.

physiology.heading: The Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Thyroid Axis and Thyroid Hormone Synthesis
points: Thyroid hormone synthesis occurs through four sequential steps within thyroid follicular cells (thyrocytes) surrounding the colloid-filled follicular lumen. First, iodide trapping: thyrocytes actively transport iodide from blood into the cell against its concentration gradient via the sodium/iodide symporter (NIS), a process directly stimulated by TSH. Second, organification: thyroid peroxidase (TPO), using hydrogen peroxide generated by the DUOX enzyme, oxidizes iodide and covalently attaches it to tyrosine residues on thyroglobulin (a large glycoprotein synthesized by thyrocytes and stored in the colloid), forming monoiodotyrosine (MIT, one iodine) and diiodotyrosine (DIT, two iodines).

Third, coupling: TPO catalyzes the joining of two iodinated tyrosine residues while still attached to the thyroglobulin backbone — coupling one MIT and one DIT forms triiodothyronine (T3), while coupling two DIT molecules forms tetraiodothyronine/thyroxine (T4); iodinated thyroglobulin is then stored extracellularly within the follicular colloid, providing a substantial hormone reserve. Fourth, release: upon TSH stimulation, thyrocytes internalize iodinated thyroglobulin from the colloid by endocytosis, lysosomal proteases digest the thyroglobulin, and the liberated T4 (roughly 80% of total secretion) and T3 (roughly 20%) are released into the fenestrated capillary network surrounding each follicle.

T4 is markedly less biologically active than T3 (often termed a prohormone), and target tissues locally regulate hormone activity via deiodinase enzymes: type 1 and type 2 deiodinases (liver, kidney, muscle, and — for type 2 — the pituitary and brain) convert T4 to the active form T3, while type 3 deiodinase (CNS, placenta) converts T4 to biologically inactive reverse T3, allowing individual tissues considerable local control over their own thyroid hormone activity independent of circulating T4/T3 ratios.

The axis is governed by classic negative feedback: hypothalamic thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) stimulates anterior pituitary thyrotrophs to secrete thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), which stimulates virtually every step of thyroid hormone synthesis described above; rising circulating T4, converted locally within pituitary thyrotrophs to T3 by type 2 deiodinase, suppresses further TSH (and TRH) release — a tightly buffered loop (aided further by high-affinity thyroid hormone-binding plasma proteins) that keeps circulating free thyroid hormone within a narrow 2-3 fold range under normal conditions.

physiology.heading: Pancreatic Islet Hormones and Glucose Homeostasis
points: Beta cells of the pancreatic islets continuously sense ambient glucose via glucose entry through GLUT2 transporters and subsequent glycolytic metabolism; the resulting rise in intracellular ATP/ADP ratio closes ATP-sensitive K+ channels, depolarizing the cell, opening voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, and triggering Ca2+-dependent exocytosis of stored insulin — glucose-stimulated insulin secretion, the primary physiological trigger for insulin release (the mechanism specifically targeted by sulfonylurea drugs, which directly close the same K+ channels).

Insulin acts through the insulin receptor, a receptor tyrosine kinase; ligand binding triggers receptor autophosphorylation and activation of the PI3K-Akt signaling cascade, which — in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue — drives translocation of GLUT4 transporters from intracellular storage vesicles to the plasma membrane, the rate-limiting step for insulin-stimulated glucose uptake in these tissues (notably, GLUT4 is largely absent from the liver, where insulin instead lowers blood glucose primarily by suppressing gluconeogenic enzyme expression and promoting glycogen synthase activity).

Glucagon, released from alpha cells predominantly in response to falling blood glucose, acts through a distinct G-protein-coupled receptor (predominantly hepatic) that activates adenylyl cyclase, raising cAMP and activating protein kinase A; PKA phosphorylates and activates glycogen phosphorylase (driving glycogenolysis) while simultaneously inhibiting glycogen synthase, and separately upregulates transcription of key gluconeogenic enzymes — the two combined mechanisms by which glucagon raises blood glucose during fasting.

Normal glucose homeostasis depends on the coordinated, reciprocal action of insulin and glucagon (secreted by adjacent cell populations within the same islet, allowing local paracrine cross-talk in addition to their systemic endocrine effects); during hypoglycemia, protection against dangerously low glucose relies on a layered defense — first reduced insulin secretion, then increased glucagon secretion, and finally (if glucose continues falling) sympathetic activation and adrenomedullary epinephrine release, which both directly stimulates hepatic glucose output and produces the adrenergic symptoms (tremor, palpitations, sweating) that typically prompt a person to recognize and treat hypoglycemia.

physiology.heading: Adrenal Steroidogenesis and the Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Adrenal Axis
points: The adrenal cortex is organized into three concentric, functionally distinct zones, each expressing a different complement of steroidogenic enzymes that determines which class of steroid hormone it can ultimately produce from the shared cholesterol precursor: the outer zona glomerulosa (uniquely expressing aldosterone synthase, producing mineralocorticoids, chiefly aldosterone, under RAAS/angiotensin II control rather than ACTH), the middle zona fasciculata (the largest zone, roughly 75% of cortical volume, its large lipid-rich 'clear cells' producing glucocorticoids, chiefly cortisol, under ACTH control), and the inner zona reticularis (compact, lipofuscin-containing cells primarily producing adrenal androgens).

The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis governs cortisol secretion: hypothalamic corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) stimulates anterior pituitary corticotrophs to release adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), which binds melanocortin 2 receptors on zona fasciculata cells, activating cAMP/PKA signaling that both acutely stimulates cortisol synthesis (by upregulating cholesterol delivery to the rate-limiting steroidogenic enzyme) and, over longer periods, promotes adrenal cortical growth. Cortisol then exerts negative feedback at both the hypothalamus (suppressing CRH) and pituitary (suppressing ACTH), while its own secretion follows a pronounced circadian rhythm — peaking in early morning and reaching its nadir near midnight — superimposed on the negative feedback loop.

Cortisol's principal metabolic actions oppose insulin's: it promotes hepatic gluconeogenesis (upregulating rate-limiting enzymes such as PEPCK and glucose-6-phosphatase), impairs peripheral GLUT4-mediated glucose uptake by disrupting insulin receptor signaling, promotes lipolysis and protein catabolism (mobilizing amino acid and fatty acid substrates for gluconeogenesis and energy production), and exerts broad anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive effects — the physiological basis for glucocorticoids' central role in the stress response, and for the metabolic derangements (hyperglycemia, muscle wasting, immunosuppression) characteristic of chronic glucocorticoid excess.

histology.heading: General Endocrine Gland Architecture
points: Endocrine glands are, by definition, ductless — they secrete their hormonal products directly into the surrounding capillary bed rather than via a duct system onto an epithelial surface, the key histological and functional distinction from exocrine glands. Consistent with this direct-to-bloodstream secretion, endocrine tissue is typically highly vascularized, often with a fenestrated capillary network permitting efficient hormone entry into circulation.

histology.heading: Thyroid Histology
points: The thyroid gland is organized into spherical follicles, each a single layer of follicular epithelial cells (cuboidal at baseline, becoming columnar under TSH stimulation, and flattened/squamous when relatively inactive) surrounding a central lumen filled with eosinophilic colloid — the extracellular storage form of iodinated thyroglobulin described in thyroid hormone synthesis physiology.

Parafollicular (C) cells, the source of calcitonin, are scattered either between follicles or within the follicular epithelium itself (typically not reaching the follicular lumen); they are somewhat larger and paler-staining than adjacent follicular cells, reflecting their distinct embryological origin (neural crest-derived, unlike the endodermally-derived follicular cells).

histology.heading: Adrenal Cortex and Medulla Histology
points: The three adrenal cortical zones are histologically distinct in addition to their functional differences: the zona glomerulosa consists of small cells arranged in tight, rounded clusters just beneath the capsule; the zona fasciculata (the thickest layer) consists of large, lipid-laden 'clear cells' (their abundant cytoplasmic lipid droplets dissolving during standard tissue processing, leaving the characteristic vacuolated, pale appearance) arranged in straight cords running perpendicular to the gland surface; and the zona reticularis consists of smaller, more compact, eosinophilic cells (lower lipid content, higher lipofuscin pigment) arranged in an irregular, net-like pattern.

The adrenal medulla, structurally and embryologically distinct from the cortex (derived from neural crest rather than mesoderm), contains chromaffin cells — modified postganglionic sympathetic neurons that, lacking postsynaptic target cells, instead release their catecholamine content (epinephrine and norepinephrine) directly into an extensive capillary network upon direct preganglionic sympathetic stimulation, consistent with the adrenal medulla's functional description as a modified sympathetic ganglion.

histology.heading: Pancreatic Islet Histology
points: The islets of Langerhans appear as small, pale-staining, well-vascularized clusters of cells scattered throughout the darker-staining exocrine acinar pancreatic tissue, readily distinguishable at low magnification by this contrast; each islet contains a mixture of hormone-producing cell types — beta cells (the most numerous, typically centrally located, producing insulin), alpha cells (typically peripheral, producing glucagon), and less numerous delta cells (producing somatostatin, which exerts local paracrine inhibitory control over both insulin and glucagon secretion within the islet).

physiology.heading: Lymphatic fluid return
points: Lymphatic capillaries collect excess interstitial fluid (as lymph) that isn't reabsorbed by blood capillaries, returning it to the venous circulation via the thoracic duct (draining most of the body) and the right lymphatic duct (draining the right upper body).
Lymph flow depends on skeletal muscle contraction, respiratory pressure changes, and one-way valves, since there is no central pumping organ analogous to the heart.
Failure of lymphatic drainage results in lymphedema, localized tissue swelling from fluid accumulation.

physiology.heading: Innate immunity
points: Innate immunity provides immediate, non-specific defense: physical/chemical barriers (skin, mucus, stomach acid), phagocytic cells (neutrophils, macrophages), natural killer cells, and the complement system.
Inflammation (heat, redness, swelling, pain) results from vasodilation and increased vascular permeability, recruiting immune cells to the site of injury/infection.
Pattern recognition receptors (e.g. Toll-like receptors) allow innate immune cells to recognize broad classes of pathogens without prior exposure.

physiology.heading: Adaptive immunity
points: Adaptive immunity is slower to develop initially but highly specific and generates immunological memory, mediated by B lymphocytes (humoral immunity, antibody production) and T lymphocytes (cell-mediated immunity).
Antigen-presenting cells (dendritic cells, macrophages) process and present antigen fragments via MHC molecules, activating antigen-specific T cell responses.
Helper T cells (CD4+) coordinate immune responses by activating B cells and cytotoxic T cells; cytotoxic T cells (CD8+) directly kill infected or abnormal cells.
Memory B and T cells persist after an initial immune response, enabling a faster, stronger response upon re-exposure to the same antigen (the basis of vaccination).

histology.heading: Lymph node structure
points: Lymph nodes have an outer cortex containing B cell-rich lymphoid follicles (some with germinal centers of actively proliferating B cells) and an inner medulla, filtering lymph as it percolates through sinuses lined with macrophages.
The paracortex, between cortex and medulla, is rich in T cells and dendritic cells, serving as a key site for antigen presentation.

histology.heading: Spleen and thymus histology
points: The spleen has red pulp (filters blood, removes aged/damaged erythrocytes, stores platelets) and white pulp (periarteriolar lymphoid sheaths and follicles, providing immune surveillance of blood-borne antigens).

The thymus is the site of T lymphocyte maturation and positive/negative selection, organized into a cortex (immature thymocytes undergoing selection) and medulla (more mature thymocytes); it is most active early in life and progressively involutes with age.

physiology.heading: Hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis
points: GnRH from the hypothalamus, released in a pulsatile fashion, stimulates LH and FSH release from the anterior pituitary.

In females, FSH stimulates ovarian follicle development and estrogen production; a mid-cycle LH surge (triggered by high estrogen via positive feedback) causes ovulation; the resulting corpus luteum secretes progesterone (and some estrogen) to maintain the uterine lining.
In males, LH stimulates testicular Leydig cells to produce testosterone; FSH acts on Sertoli cells to support and regulate spermatogenesis.
Continuous (non-pulsatile) GnRH exposure paradoxically suppresses the axis — the physiological basis for GnRH agonist therapies.

physiology.heading: The menstrual cycle
points: The follicular phase (variable length) is characterized by rising estrogen from the developing dominant follicle, driving endometrial proliferation.
Ovulation occurs roughly at cycle midpoint, triggered by the LH surge.

The luteal phase (relatively fixed ~14 days) is dominated by progesterone from the corpus luteum, which prepares the endometrium for potential implantation; without fertilization/implantation, the corpus luteum regresses, hormone levels fall, and menstruation follows.

physiology.heading: Gametogenesis
points: Spermatogenesis occurs continuously from puberty onward within the seminiferous tubules, progressing through spermatogonia, primary/secondary spermatocytes, spermatids, and mature spermatozoa, taking roughly 64-72 days.

Oogenesis begins during fetal development, with oocytes arrested in prophase of meiosis I until puberty; typically one oocyte per cycle resumes and completes meiosis I (arresting again in meiosis II) around ovulation, only completing meiosis II if fertilized.

histology.heading: Testicular histology
points: Seminiferous tubules are lined by a complex, stratified epithelium of developing germ cells at sequential maturation stages, interspersed with Sertoli (supporting) cells that nourish developing sperm and form the blood-testis barrier.
Leydig cells, located in the interstitial tissue between tubules, produce testosterone under LH stimulation.

histology.heading: Ovarian histology
points: Ovarian follicles at different developmental stages (primordial, primary, secondary, mature/Graafian) are found within the ovarian cortex, each comprising an oocyte surrounded by granulosa cells (and later, theca cells).
The corpus luteum, formed from the ruptured follicle after ovulation, is a temporary endocrine structure with large, lipid-rich luteal cells producing progesterone.

physiology.heading: Thermoregulation
points: Eccrine sweat gland secretion and evaporative cooling are the primary mechanisms for heat loss in hot conditions or during exercise, controlled by the hypothalamic thermoregulatory center via sympathetic cholinergic fibers.
Cutaneous vasodilation increases blood flow to the skin surface, promoting radiant/convective heat loss; vasoconstriction conserves core heat in cold conditions by shunting blood away from the skin.
Arrector pili muscles cause piloerection ('goosebumps'), a largely vestigial thermoregulatory response in humans that would trap an insulating air layer in more densely-furred mammals.
Shivering thermogenesis (involuntary rapid muscle contraction) generates metabolic heat as a cold response, coordinated by the hypothalamus.

physiology.heading: Barrier and protective functions
points: The stratum corneum (outermost epidermal layer) forms the primary physical barrier against water loss and pathogen entry, via tightly packed, keratin-filled dead corneocytes and intercellular lipids.
Melanin, produced by melanocytes and transferred to keratinocytes, absorbs and scatters UV radiation, protecting underlying DNA from UV-induced damage.
The skin's acidic surface pH and resident normal flora contribute to defense against pathogenic colonization.

physiology.heading: Sensory and metabolic functions
points: The skin contains diverse sensory receptors: Meissner's corpuscles (light touch), Pacinian corpuscles (deep pressure/vibration), Merkel cells (sustained touch), free nerve endings (pain, temperature) — making it the body's largest sensory organ.
Vitamin D synthesis begins in the skin: UVB radiation converts 7-dehydrocholesterol to previtamin D3, which is subsequently processed by the liver and kidneys into active calcitriol.

histology.heading: Epidermal layers
points: The epidermis is stratified squamous keratinized epithelium, organized (from deep to superficial) into stratum basale (mitotically active stem cells), stratum spinosum, stratum granulosum, (stratum lucidum, in thick skin only), and stratum corneum (dead, keratin-filled corneocytes).
Keratinocytes, the dominant epidermal cell type, migrate outward and differentiate as they progress toward the surface, ultimately being shed (desquamation).

Melanocytes reside in the stratum basale, extending processes to transfer melanin to surrounding keratinocytes; Langerhans cells (antigen-presenting immune cells) and Merkel cells (mechanoreceptor-associated) are also found within the epidermis.

histology.heading: Dermis and hypodermis
points: The dermis, beneath the epidermis, is divided into the papillary layer (loose connective tissue, forms dermal papillae interlocking with the epidermis) and the reticular layer (dense irregular connective tissue, rich in collagen and elastic fibers).
The dermis contains blood vessels, nerve endings, hair follicles, sebaceous glands, and sweat glands.

The hypodermis (subcutaneous layer), technically not part of the skin proper, is composed mostly of adipose tissue, providing insulation, energy storage, and cushioning, and anchors the skin to underlying fascia/muscle.
